On section 1-tenure of office of chief commissioner if ex-judge.

-Apparently it is the intention of the government to go on with this proposition and to recognize the principle of the promotion of judges. In a former discussion in this House I tried to show that it was bad policy to introduce this principle in this country, and I still hold the samd opinion. The ends of justice will be better served if those who are appointed judges remain where they are, if hopes of translation to other boards or courts are not held out to them, if once they have taken office they concentrate their efforts entirely upon the interpretation of the law and the doing of justice, instead of trying to earn promotion to some other sphere where the emolument is greater. Bearing on that, I wish to read the opinion of a newspaper which is supposed to reflect the sentiments of the farmers of this country. Last week the ' Weekly Sun ' said :
Is it desirable that judges should he open to promotion by the government of the day ? To ask the question, it seems to us, is to answer it. The courts must be free from any suspicion of subjection to political pressure, and how can such freedom exist if judges can be promoted at the will of the government ? Give to an administration power to advance a judge who strains the laiy to favour the party in power in an election trial, and we shall at once have all the evils of an elective judiciary with none of the advantages of that system.
Once a man is appointed to a seat on ihe bench it should be clearly understood by all concerned that he has nothing further to hope for or fear at the hands of the government of the day.
This utterance, which is supposed to reflect the opinion of the every-day farmer and the ordinary citizen of this country, expresses good policy. It is on the line of the precedent established in the old country. It is in the public interest that our judges should not have the chance of being promoted to offices with higher salaries, but that they should concentrate their whole lives to the doing of justice in the sphere in which they are placed. Hon. gentlemen opposite have asked, should a judge not aspire to promotion ? I say he should not ; I say that the door ought to be shut on such aspirations. True, this may be somewhat detrimental to the judge ; but it is not the hopes or prospects of the judge that ought to govern us, but the doing of justice and the maintaining of the integrity of the bench, which is of much higher concern to the people of this country. I leave that point -simply with that statement, and I go on to the next point, that is, that the government propose to make the chairman of the Railway Commission removable only upon an address of the Senate and House of Commons. This is a direct reversal of the policy that was laid down here by the government when they passed the Railway Act through this House. When they introduced the Bill
to establish a railway commission consisting of the chairman and two assistant commissioners, they said : we do not intend to have these men placed as judges, but as lieutenant governors. The Hon. Mr. Blair, when introducing the Bill-said this :
The opinion of council, in going over the Bill,
was that it would be desirable to place the members of the commission very much in the same position as lieutenant governors under the British North America Act. It is a very cumbrous proceeding to invite the action of the Senate and House of Commons by an address. Cases might arise in which it would be very important and desirable that prompt action should he taken without waiting for a session of parliament.
Yet the proposal now is to absolutely reverse the policy that was then laid down as being in the public interest. I will Quote from what Mr. Blair said in that respect:
The Bill which we submitted last year contained, and the present Bill, when printed, will be found to contain a clause providing that the members of the commission are only removable on an address of both Houses of parliament to the Governor General. This, on full consideration, we concluded to change, and although the Bill when it is distributed will contain such a clause, it is an oversight which will he remedied iu the committee. We propose that the members of the commission shall be removable in the same manner as the lieutenant governors of the provinces, namely, by the Governor General in Council for cause.
Now, I think the government are bound to give a reason for this reversal of policy. They said they wanted to have the members of this Railway Commission occupy the same status as lieutenant governors and they took power to the Governor in Council to remove them for cause. Now they are introducing a Bill to provide that the chief commissioner, if he happens to be a judge, can be removed only on an address of both Houses of parliament. A very interesting incident came up in the Railway Committee room this morning. We were discussing how the public might be relieved from certain conditions that exist in connection with railways, and it was argued w ith great vehemence by railway representatives that this Railway Commission was not only judicial but legislative.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In what respect is it legislative ?

Read the Act in any of its sections almost, and you will find evidence of my statement. Take clause 25 :
The board may make orders and regulations limiting the rate of speed at which railway trains and locomotives may run in any city, town or village or any class of cities, towns or villages described in any regulation ; and if the board thinks fit the rate of speed within certain described portions of any city, town or village, and allowing another rate of speed in other portions thereof.
Section 25 (f). The board may make orders and regulations with respect to the rolling stock

apparatus, cattle guards, appliances, signals, methods, devices, structures and works, to he used upon the railway so as to provide means tor the due protection of property, the employees of the company and the public.
All through that Act, this railway company is given practically legislative powers. The Minister of Railways argued all morning in the Railway Committee that great power in matters of legislation were practically vested in this Railway Commission. Then I come to this point, which I commend to the right hon. gentleman who says he has always been an apostle of responsible government. Where you have legislative powers conferred on anybody, ought not that body to be responsible ? If this Railway Commission is vested with legislative powers and functions, it should be responsible to parliament, and it was with that intention that the law was made as it passed two years ago. Mr. Blair's argument was that the only way in which you could keep a check on this Railway Commission and compel it to discharge its duties was to make it responsible to parliament, that was why the commissioners were made removable by Order of the Governor General in Council, and in thus limiting their tenure of office, their conduct could he discussed in this House and relief obtained where required. If the conduct of these commissioners is subject to discussion in this House, then the responsibility will rest on the government either to remove them, if the House has censured their administration or change the law. It seems to me that the public interest demands that this commission should be kept' as it is * and the chairman, as well as every other member of that commission, be removable by Order of the Governor General in Council. I make the charge boldly that the government, by tliis amendment to the Railway Act which they are asking us to pass, are reversing their policy. Now that the elections are over, they are taking a step backwards in the interests of the railway companies ; and because I brought Judge Killam's name into the debate, not in any spirit of criticism as regards that gentleman, who justly holds a high place in the judiciary, but because I thought that the government were not justified in placing the chairman of the commission, whether he might be judge Klllam or anybody else, in a different position from that provided under the present law, the right hon. gentleman said I was casting a slur on a distinguished member of the bench. I was not doing anything of the kind, but the right hon. gentleman and his government are casting a slur on the policy they adopted two years ago. and which they led the public to believe Would be maintained.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend will of course understand that when I say I cannot do better than refer him to the debate Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
that has already occurred for an answer no discourtesy is intended. Almost everything my hon. friend lias just said was then argued with equal force* and emphasis, and I then endeavoured to reply as well as I could. My hon. friend knows the views I hold in common with himself respecting the promotion of judges meets with my entire approval, but the views he and I hold in common do not appear to have got beyond the apostolic stage. We are both apostles of a new idea, and new ideas do not advance as rapidly as we would like. In this country the principle of no promotion for a judge lias never been accepted or acted upon, nor has it been acted upon in England to any great extent. It has been stated in England in the abstract, but has not been lived up to. In the present instance however, we are not dealing with the question of promotion, but with the question of the translation of judges from one sphere to another.
We transfer the judge from the position of judge of the Supreme Court to the position of chairman of the Railway Commission. That brings me to the other question my hon. friend brought up-the question of tenure of office. I understand him to put his argument in this way: It was intended, when this Railway Act was introduced, to make these Railway Commissioners practically controllable by parliament; the intention was that their conduct might be discussed in parliament with greater freedom than would be possible if they were judges. But I would point out that there is nothing here that departs from the principle laid down in the Railway Act. We do not depart from the principle of removal of members of the commission by the Governor in Council. We maintain that principle. But with respect to one particular class of persons, the judges of this land, we provide that if one of them is taken from his court and made chairman of the Railway Commission, his tenure of office should continue as it was before. It is not a question whether the chairman of the Railway Commission shall or shall not be removable by vote of parliament, but it is a question whether or not we shall take to ourselves the right to extend the sphere within which we may select our chairman of the commission, and whether we shall or shall not so arrange our legislation as to put us in a position to go to our judges and say to them: We can requisition your services for this position without in any way interfering with your tenure of office. We do not go beyond that. We do not say that if a layman is made chairman of the commission he shall not be removable by the Governor in Council, or that the two other commissioners shall not be so removable. The general rule with regard to the tenure of office remains the same; all we say is that if we hapen to take a judge as chairman of the commission then, with regard to that particular individual, his tenure of office as

1605T
judge shall not be altered. I hope my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) understands that. These are the facts. If he misapprehends the Bill, it may be because he has studied newspaper reports about the Bill, rather than the Bill itself.
Will the hon. minster permit me to answer him in one word?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.

The hon. minister says that this is an exception, and an individual case. I venture the prediction that every appointment hereafter will be of a judge from the bench, so that from this time forward-and that is the intention of the Bill-this principle shall always apply to the chairman of the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, my hon. friend will realize that my obligation is to deal with the Bill and not with his predictions. The hon. minister is begging the whole question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I put the question if not to my hon. friend, to the House for his benefit. Does the general principle of appointment and tenure of office remain the same as before?
Will the hon. minister allow me to ask him a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Does not it follow that under this exception the general principle can be ignored for ever in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend has not answered my question, but I will answer his. The general principle remains the same as before. If, in the future, instead of asking a judge to become chairman of the commission, we choose a chairman from the bar, or from outside the legal profession, he will be removable by the Governor in Council. There is no use in dealing with predictions about it. We have to take the responsibilities' for the legislation we have introduced, But we want the legislation to be understood, and we want the House to pass upon the measure and not upon some misapprehension of the measure.
This is class legislation with a vengeance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It may be so in the view of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) but, of course, I cannot be expected to take that view. But, I would like to state my case in the meantime

Will the minister answer this question: Suppose that two other commissioners are appointed under the same tenure of office as this chairman, what would become of the general principle of appointment ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: It is confined them, to the chief commissioner ? I thought it applied to all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is confined absolutely to the chief commissioner. And there is a reason for that. The chairman, so far as questions of law are concerned, is the supreme arbiter. His ruling upon a question of law is binding upon the commission. Therefore, it is desirable that we should have a man in that position-that honourable and important position-who has not only the necessary legal attainments, but, in addition, has had judicial experience. AVe think that, under certain conditions, this may prove most desirable. The chairman practically plays the part of a judge. From his judgment on points of iaw there are few appeals, and these under most restricted conditions. Now, we say, that, in order to enable us to secure the services of such a man, it is desirable to amend the law in this particular. I do not think I can add anything to this, I fear I have wearied the House by repeating what I have said before. But let the legislation be understood. I do not want the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). -I say it without any discourtesy-to misrepresent the Bill, or hon. members generally to decide upon anything except the Bill itself.

I rise with some diffidence to speak upon this question, for certainly it is a question of difficulty. I do



not think it is free from doubt whichever way you look at it. Having given it consideration both when it was put before the House and to-day, and having listened to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick), I am obliged to say that, in my opinion, the departure now being made is attended with danger. It is quite true that this Bill applies only to the chief commissioner. But, that being the case it applies to one who, as the Minster of Justice has said is in the position of a supreme arbitrator. A good deal of discussion has taken place throughout the country as to the peculiar and special powers that are given to the chief commissioner. But I apprehend that is absolutely necessary that these powers should be intrusted to the one who occupies that position. In this commission we have virtually two courts sitting, a court of three for the trial of questions of facts, and a court of one for the trial of questions of law. We must confine the decision of these cases of law, in the first instance, to some one who has a knowledge of law and is able to decide them. [DOT] But all the same, we are giving this chief commissioner a great deal of power, very much more than we are giving to any' of the others, and in proportion as we are giving him more power it is essential that we should be in a position, whatever his feelings might be, to control those powers in the interest of the country, in case it should happen-and that is possible, though not probable-that he does not appear to be acting in the interest of the country. There can be a great deal said in favour of the legislation that is now proposed. It is the same class of legislation that we are applying, as I understand, to the Auditor General. Is that correct ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

In the case of the Auditor General, we have on many occasions pointed out the great benefit of the system we there adopted. I am convinced yet that it is a benefit. The difficulty that I see is this, that it removes to some extent the control that we have over the chief commissioner, and introduces what I regard as a great danger, the danger of political influence. In the case of the Anditor General there is no great power that can be rallied by him in his support so that he can virtually defy parliament. There is no great power that can be rallied against him so as to do him an injustice, or do the people an injustice by dismissing him when he is there in the interest of the people. But in the case of a chief commissioner who is controlling to a large extent the great railways and corporate interests of the country, there can be a lobby of such stupendous influence invoked as has never been presented probably upon any occasion in this House of Commons. When a question arises in this House we are confronted with great corporate interests, but usually by a corpo-Mr. LENNOX.
rate interest of one great railway alone, and fortunately for the balance of power, we have another great corporate interest, another great railway company, probably minimizing to some extent the influence of the other. But when we come to deal with these we have the possibility of that kind, the corporate influence of all the great railways of this country, and they are growing greater every year. We may have the influence of all the great railways on the one side and the people demanding a dismissal upon the other ; and I venture to say, without any reflection upon parliament or upon any member thereof now sitting here or who may sit here, that it is not in the interest of this country, at least it is very questionable whether it is in the interest of this country, that we should have an official as commissioner in that position, as regards our right of removal. It is a very serious question, one of the most serious which parliament has been confronted with. It is a very radical departure from the principle upon which this matter was introduced in the first instance. It is a departure as to the appointment and control of at least a third of the commission, yes, more than a third, because it is the chief commissioner that has most control, the one who interprets the law. He has three-fourths as much power as the power of the ether two combined. Therefore, though I do not want to be extreme, because I recognize the importance of looking at this matter calmly, still I desire to call attention to the1 fact that a great question is at issue here, and it behooves us to be careful In what we do. We may be confronted in the near future with the position of having a commissioner whom we virtually have not power to remove in the way that is proposed. Now, let me point out one other thing that probably several lion, gentlemen have thought of, though I do not think it has been mentioned. We might have this position of things, we might have a judge, or there might be in the eye of some administration a person for this position who is not a judge, but there is nothing to prevent them making him a judge, and so translating him from a judgeship to a commis-sionersliip in order to make him come within this provision. The Minister of Justice has said, and no doubt sincerely, that it only applies to a case where we remove a gentleman from the position of a judge and put him In this position, but we can put a gentleman in the position of a judge and within a week, or a month, or a year, remove him to the position of chief commissioner, and then this law applies to him. So you see what vast power, what vast political influence can be invoked under this provision. I do not mean for a moment * that the administration have that object in view, that is not my view of the matter.
I say that I wish to approach this statute exactly in the way the Minister of Justice says we should, and to deal with it after

looking at all possible eventualities. I am surely within the judgment of this committee when I say that this is a difficulty that may arise.

speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) supposes a case where the government, in order to bring a commissioner within the provision of this Act, might appoint a person as judge for the purpose of raising him to the office of commissioner. Now, my hon. friend is not forgetting the fact that the best control you have over any ruling or any decision given by the board is the fact that the same Governor in Council can, on appeal, set any one of these rulings aside. That is the best control you can exercise. It is not necessary that they should cancel the commissioner's appointment. If an improper ruling is made by the commissioners, all that a person who has suffered has to do is to take up the Railway Act, look at section 44 and he will find that the Governor in Council has power to amend or rescind that ruling on appeal. What more effective control could you have than that ?

I would like to say that I think this Bill has many objections and presents a great danger. It seems to me that we are consecrating by legislation the principle of the promotion of judges, and thereby incurring the danger that has been mentioned by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean). It is sufficient to look at a paragraph in the clause under consideration to see that it involves the consecration of the principle of the promotion of judges, a principle which has never been admitted in England.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it has been admitted,
It has bipen departed from on rare occasions and departed from here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not' on rare occasions.

On rather rare occasions. I would go the full length of what my, hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has said ; I would not be prepared to admit the principle that a judge can be promoted, even in his own court, to the presidency of the court. The hon. Minister of Justice knows better than I do that this question has given rise to a great deal of discussion. I do not think you can find a single statute where the principle is as clearly enunciated as it is in this Bill we now have under consideration. Besides that, the hon. Minister of Justice has himself intimated that we probably will follow that practice. It was not a prediction that my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) made. He was arguing from the inconvenience that would be caused in the future by this Bill if carried, and the hon. Minister of Justice himself says that we require as the president of this tribunal a man who not only knows the law, but who is accustomed to the judicial interpretation of the law. That is an intimation, a very natural one, but a very clear intimation, that not only will we con-

secrate the principle of the promotion of those who are called upon to discharge these functions, but it is probable that in future we will not only choose men who have a knowledge of the law, but men who are accustomed to the exeycise of judicial functions. Of course, I quite recognize that the possibility of anything such as was suggested by the hon. gentleman who spoke before me is a very remote one. I do not think, as the hon. Minister of Justice has said, that we will at any time-although we see very extraordinary things nowadays -place a lawyer upon the bench to transfer him immediately to this important position, but I think it presents a danger of a different kind, and it is more than probable that if this policy is consecrated by the House, and if what was intimated by the hon. Minister' of Justice is carried out, this position may become a shelving position, a place where we will shelve judges who have had some experience on the bench, and I think the principle that we are now called upon to consecrate is a dangerous one. But I would like further to call the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice to this anomaly : We are establishing by this Bill a varying tenure of office. If we take a judge and place him in that position, making him independent of the executive, we are establishing a peculiar and special tenure of office. I am very far from disapproving of that principle ; I think it is an excellent one. I would argue that the members who compose this commission ought to be in that position. Upon that point I differ from my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean). I revert to the old principle establed by the Settlement Act in 1701. Judges occupying high positions, occupying seats in the superior courts, ought all to be placed in the position that they cannot be removed except upon the joint address of both Houses. My hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) says that they are not open to criticism if we give them that tenure of office. They are. Judges can be criticised in this House freely. Their decisions are open to criticism by the representatives of the people, but their removal from office can only be subject to this important condition that the executive can only act upon the address of both Houses. Is that a too protected position to give men occupying seats upon what I would call a most important tribunal in the country I do not think so ; in fact, I would almost argue- although this view is one which I have not carefully considered-that according to the spirit of our Constitutional Act of 1867. if not according to the letter, they have the right to that protection, because, if I remember the section well, all judges or superior tribunals are named by the federal authorities, and can only be removed on a joint address of both Houses. I would go to the length of saying that if the federal authority creates the tribunals that are called the superior courts, the judges are en-Mr. MONK.
titled to that protection. But my hon. friend the Minister of Justice sees what my objection is. It makes the tenure of office a varying one. If the office has been occupied by a judge for several years, it may afterwards be occupied by a man who has not had a seat on the bench, and who will be removable at will. I think that is objectionable. We ought to fix the tenure of office in an irrevocable way, and I am quite prepared to accept the tenure of office which I think would be the most suitable for a man occupying a position of that kind. There is another point of some importance worth the consideration of the committee, and it is this : Not only is the tenure of office of the chief commissioner a varying one, but it differs from that of the two other judges, if I may call them judges. I think they are. In the case of a judge being promoted to this position, he is in that position of independence which has always been considered, since the beginning of the eighteenth century, a matter of the supremest importance. He is independent of the executive, but his two colleagues who sit with him, whose jurisdiction is the same, except in one particular pointed out by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and who ought to be, I submit to this committee, in the same position of independence as the president of the tribunal, are in a very different position indeed. They are subservient to the executive and can be removed by the government. At any rate, they do not occupy that position of independence, which, under the special circumstances contemplated by this Bill, is assigned to the chief commissioner. I think that is very objectionable. I think the three members of the tribunal, although their attributes may differ in the particular pointed out by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, ought to be placed on the same basis of independence. I do not know whether I expressed that opinion last year when the Bill was up for consideration, but my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will remember that the discussion upon that Bill was very long, and I, for one, would be of the opinion that they all ought to be placed under the same tenure of office. These men are called upon to decide most important questions. Their jurisdiction covers matters involving thousands and millions of dollars and, from a material point of view, they are occupied with things of far greater monetary value, as a rule, than are any of the other tribunals of the country. I think, under these circumstances, they are subject, as all judges are. to dangerous influences, and to render them perfectly independent I do not think we could do better than to apply to them that very important principle which was adopted in England at the time it was first consecrated in the Settlement Act.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to find that the principle I advocated when

tlie resolutions were first introduced to the House seems to be very unanimously supported by both sides of the House. The principle may be departed from in some instances in Great Britain and perhaps in this country, but it is the principle which underlies the appointment of all judges in any part or portion of the empire, particularly in the Dominion, that when a man gets the appointment of judge he must expect to remain in that position for the full tenure of his office and must expect no promotion. If you depart from that principle once then you' offer to the judge an opportunity of becoming a political partisan, because the support of a political partisan may give him promotion from one court to another. However, I am glad to find out that that principle of mine is supported by the Minister of Justice and is very generally adopted throughout the House. Now as to the other point, the tenure of office of judges when this Bill-I may call it an extraordinary BUI-gave to some gentlemen in this country greater powers than are given to any other gentlemen that I know of in any other part or portion of the world, it was intended to give them greater powers. When the exMinister of Railways introduced the Bill he intended to make this a court, and if I remember rightly, the commissioners were not to be removed without cause and only by address of both Houses of parliament. I protested, and if I remember rightly the right hon. gentleman who leads the government agreed with me. that the appointment should be during good behaviour or subject to removal by the Governor in Council. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) says that we have ministerial responsibility for this now, in the matter of appointment. What we wanted when the Bill was passed was to have legislative control over every action of that commission, and to have them directly responsible to this House through ministerial responsibility. You appoint a man who is only removable by addresses- of both Houses of parliament and to that extent the right hon. gentleman who leads the government at the present day is relieved from any ministerial responsibility in the case. The Minister of Justice.says 'no,' we retained that under the Bill ; we have the power of revising any judgment that is given by this commission from time to time and of altering and amending it. They have on their own motion, if I understand the Bill, power to revise any judgment of the commission. The Minister of Justice would argue that that ministerial responsibility continues. How does it continue ? Suppose they alter, amend or find fault with the judgment of the chief commissioner. How are they to punish him ? He is not removable by the Governor in Council : he will go on giving the same opinions from time to time, forever. The anomaly of it is this: there are two parties on this commission who are directly responsible to this House and to the country for all their judgments ; there is one whose tenure of office is entirely different, who is placed in the position of a judge, and whose opinions this House has no way of correcting, judging, altering or doing anything to unless there is some cijuse and an address is made by both Houses of parliament finding fault with him and asking for his removal. That is exactly the position in reference to the chief commissioner who is placed in the position of a judge. I differ from my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) altogether, in reference to the contention that these parties ought to be given the powers of judges. For exceptional reasons extraordinary powers were given to the judgeg of this country ; for the interpretation of the laws, for the decision between the government of the country and the individual and for a great many other reasons the judges of the country have to be entirely independent of political pressure, of the pressure of the government or of legislative pressure of any kind. This is an entirely different court. This is a court which primarily was in the hands of the legislature altogether, through its representatives, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. For anything that the Railway Committee of the Privy Council did they were as directly responsible to parliament as it was possible to be. Is a chief commissioner appointed under this Act, with the tenure of office which is given him under this Bill, in that position ? I contend that he is in an entirely different one and that there is no reason under this Bill to change or alter the tenure of office of the party who is chief commissioner. It may have been difficult for the government to get a chief commissioner who will have their confidence who is well known to be an excellent judge and fitted in every respect for the office. If you have such a man, give him the position, make provision if necessary for his retiring allowance, but do not alter the tenure of office, do not deprive this government nor this legislature of the power of control exercised by the Railway Commission as appointed by this Act. Do not take away part of the powers of the legislature because this is nothing else than taking away part of the powers of this House, exercised in giving them a different tenure of office.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Hnggart) argues for ministerial responsibility with respect to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. My hon. friend will realize at a glance that the whole principle of the Railway Act under which the board was created, is a departure from that principle. The old Railway Committee of the Privy Council carried otft the idea which my hon. friend had in mind. It was in operation for a great many years, but in 1003 it was decided that we' should depart

from that principle and adopt the principle of a Board of Railway Commissioners, independent of parliament altogether, except in so far as parliament might exercise control over the commissioners in two respects, through the Governor in Council- mark you there is no direct control but control through the Governor in Council in two respects, first, in respect to the control in so far as appointment and tenure of office went, and then only in case they misbehave because their tenure of office was subject to their good behaviour. In addition to that parliament desired that that parliamentary control which my hon. friend speaks of should be exercised by the Governor in Council in the most absolute manner under section 44, I think it is, of the Railway Act, which provided that the Governor in Council not only should sit as a Court of Appeal, but that the Governor in Council should of his own motion have the right to interfere and to alter, vary or change any order made by the board. Now you have, in so far as control is concerned, the same supreme control over the action of the commissioners through the Governor in Council as you had before this Bill was introduced. There is no departure from that. What is the use of beating the air or fighting with windmills over this ?

Who is the wind-mill ?
Mr. FITZPATRICK/ Let us realize what we are doing. We are now, Mr. Speaker, dealing with a concrete case, and my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) if I have understood, his argument correctly, agreed so far as the principle is concerned with respect to the particular appointment, but said: ' Make provision with respect to the particular appointment in the way you have provided, but do not make the principle general. Now we have departed from his view in this respect, that we have applied the principle to a class of persons and he wants to have It applied only to the individual. There is where I differ from my hon. friend from South Lanark.

The Minister of Justice argues that when we passed the Railway Act we made a departure altogether from our usual method of trying these cases. I differ from him entirely, and if he will follow his own argument afterwards he will see tlie fallacy of it. It was only for the convenience of the Privy Council that we delegated to the commission the right of inquiry into these cases. The Minister of Justice says the residue of power is in the Privy Council, and, therefore, there is a responsibility to parliament. Then the argument of the Minister of Justice fails altogether. Here is a court appointed for the convenience of the Privy Council, and there is no giving away of any power which the Privy Council had in the past, only a delegation of power. The Privy Council retains Mr. FITZPATRICK.
the power all the time, and, as the Minister of Justice says, is responsible for the judgment of the commission. Parliament intended that this commission should be controlled by this legislature, but if you appoint to the commission parties who are in no way responsible to the government for their conduct, then you vary the power and control which this House had hitherto over the commission.

It has been contended in this House that the members of this commission are judges. They may be judges; I would not altogether dispute that, but they are more than judges. To them parliament has delegated the power to legislate in regard to railways, and I hold that when parliament has delegated powers it ought to have control. Parliament has retained control over all the commissioners except the chairman. The hon. Minister of Justice says that this case is an exception, and I wish to describe exactly what it is. This legislation is a reversal of the general principle by an exception that can be made continuous, that is, a complete reversal of policy. I have no doubt that it will be made continuous, and that for all time we shall have the chairman of the commission holding his office under a different tenure from that of his colleagues. Again, if we delegate parliamentary powers to these commissioners, making them more than commissioners, we ought to hold them in our hands as we did under the original law. But that is now changed in reference to the chairman of the commission, who happens to be a judge. I do not want to say anything personal, but I wish to ask if Mr. Justice ICillam asked for this change ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether he asked for the change or not. I know that we offered him the office and he has accepted. More than that, he is a most desirable appointment.

He is a most desirable appointment, and I would like to see Mr. Justice Killam accept the office under the original conditions, and under them give the country the benefit of his valuable services. I agree with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that it wouid be better to increase the salary in this case than to consecrate, as we are doing, the principle that judges may be promoted.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion in regard to the character of this commission, on which a great deal might be said. I do not agree that the commission was instituted in order to relieve the administration of administrative work. A his question has been studied a great deal in the United States and England, and I think that a perusal of what has been written on the subject will show that, on the contrary, the object of the institution of a Railway Commission is to remove the decision of cases

from the executive and to bring them under judicial consideration by making the Railway Commission a kind of tribunal. That being the view I take, I still think we ought to go the whole length and apply this tenure of office not only to the president of the commission, but to all its members, on account of the immense importance of the questions submitted to them and of the nature of their functions. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice is perhaps able to say what was the tenure of office of the British Railway Commissioners. My recollection of what happened in England is that a railway commission was resorted to, but did not operate satisfactorily and has since been abandoned. Has my hon. friend the Minister of Justice had occasion to learn what was the tenure of office of the Railway Commissioners in England.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There were three appointed commissioners and two ex-officio -one each for England, Ireland and Scotland, and they Lad always to be superior court judges. In England the chief commissioner was the Lord Chancellor, in Ireland the Lord Chancellor of Ireland and in Scotland the Lord President of the Court of Session; that is, they took as chief commissioner the highest judical officer in the country. The term of office is for life.

I thank the Minister of Justice for That information. My hon. friend from South York must see that in England they consider the functions of these men as essentially judicial functions, and they are all protected-they cannot be removed without the intervention of parliament.
The debate, as far as it has gone, seems to establish a few very plain facts. One is that we had a chairman of the Railway Commission and that we are now without him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend has the habit of being exceedingly accurate, but he knows that the statement is not correct. We have a chairman now.
We are making a further appointment under this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have made it.

Another point that is apparent is that the business of the country suffered by reason of the way the office was vacated. The chairman of the Railway Commission was a man of undoubted ability. He has dealt with very many important matters, and many other's were under consideration. These matters were in an unfinished state at the time he left the office. Without any apparent reason the office was vacated.
The business of the country, so far as this commission is concerned, has been at a standstill for upwards of three mouths, and what the country wants to know is who is going to pay the immense damage caused by this delay. This Bill takes no
cognizance of the main point which has been brought out by the experience of the past. That experience has shown that a man appointed to a high ftffice can lay it down at a moment's notice without paying to the country any damage for the losses caused by his conduct. Because the chairman of the Railway Commission gave up his high office at a moment's notice, the business of the country has had to suffer, yet we are now proposing to make a new appointment without taking any means to prevent the recurrence of similar conduct. The new appointment we are hedging about with every safeguard, so far as the incumbent is concerned. We are promoting a man from a judgeship to be the head of that commission. I know nothing of the ability of the gentleman appointed. He may be everything he is declared to be, and I take it for granted he is, but I would like to point out that the business of the country is no more safeguarded in this proposed legislation than it is in the present law. I read over the Bill carefully and I cannot find in it 3ny attempt to guard against a repetition of what has just occurred. Would the directors of any railway system appoint a man to manage that system and leave him perfectly free to resign without a moment's notice, either because he did not like the job or because he wanted to avoid some unpleasant or difficult business, or for any other reason, and leave him free to do so without giving any explanation and without their having any recourse against him. Under this Bill, it will be very difficult, almost impossible, to remove the chairman of that commission, but there will be n'o difficulty whatever on his part in laying it down. It seems to me that a safeguard should be provided so that he could not resign office without the consent of parliament. Parliament makes the appointment, and the consent of parliament should be required before he can he relieved of the office. I draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to that fact. We have had a long debate on the appointment of judges, but I have yet to hear any satisfactory explanation why the chairman should be at liberty to lay down the office without giving due notice, notwithstanding that important matters may have come before him and be awaiting his decision. A great deal of expense and loss and inconvenience has been caused by the resignation of the late chairman. That gentleman was a man of high standing, who commanded the confidence of the public, while he presided in that court. So fay as I am concerned, I always looked upon him as a higher authority than any hon. gentlemen opposite on railway questions, and particularly on the question of the cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. I looked upon him as an authority and the country did also.
Up to what date ?

Up to November, 1904. He certainly was an able man, but he held bis position onlj^ a brief time. During that time he had travelled a good deal about the country and heard many cases and in .many 0f these cases had not given judgment. But apparently without any reason, he lay down this office, and we are now proceeding to make an appointment in his place. But in making this appointment we are not benefiting by the experience of the past. That experience should teach us to require of the new incumbent due notice of his intention to leave the office and due responsibility for any damage which his sudden resignation might cause parties interested. I trust that the Minister of Justice will consider the point I have raised and consider it in the same spirit as that in which I submit it. The gentleman who has received the appointment may be as eminent and learned as we are told he is. but what guarantee have we that lie will not vacate his office without first obtaining our consent. We cannot remove him, but he may remove us. We cannot hold him, but he can hold us in the hollow of his hand, and he can step down and out at any moment without any regard to the business of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: , My hon. friend, no doubt, has considered this matter, as he does all matters, with a great deal of care. But he must not lose sight of the fact that if the chairman of the Railway Commission lays down his office before the expiring of the time fixed, he will loose his retiring allowance. If in addition, my hon. friend will give us the benefit of his business experience and suggest anything else we can do, I shall be very glad to consider his suggestion.

I would suggest that he should give due notice of his resignation, so that the government may have some opportunity of putting some one in his place before he leaves the office. He could very well give due notice. He should be required to give decisions also in the cases he has had in hand. It seems to me that we ought to be able to make some provision which will prevent the holder of that office from giving it up without a moment's notice, leaving the business before the court unsettled, and saddling the parties interested with the delay and expense of going all over the proceedings again, and yet not be liable in the slightest degree to any penalty or damage.

The point to which my hon. friend has called attention is most important. No doubt the resignation of Mr. Blair is the only instance we have had of a man holding high office, throwing it up without giving any notice and without any regard to the cases that were pending before him. That is no doubt the only instance of the kind in our history, Mr. COCKSHUTT.
but it has had the worst possible effect on the morale of the whole service of the country. We have had the chairman of this Railway Commission resigning that office without warning, leaving a lot of unfinished business behind which he, as a judge sworn to do his duty, should have had completed, and doing this without any explanation. If the contention made by the Minister of Justice to-day is correct, the Minister of Justice and his colleagues are responsible for that Railway Commission.
I say, an explanation is due the country why that officer resigned. And there ought to be provision, whether in this law or in the general law against a recurrence of such a thing. It is a most deplorable thing, and some notice ought to be taken of it, some reprobation passed upon it. It is worthy of a resolution of this House, and perhaps such a resolution may be introduced this session. The case is that of a man holding the greatest office in this country abandoning that office, refusing to give judgment in cases he had heard, yet giving no reason for his conduct. And those who are responsible for his appointment and for the execution of the duties of that office have given no explanation. This is an injury to the public morals. The thing will not down. Those who are responsible must discharge their responsibility and explain the conduct of this man ; or if they are not in a position to explain it, they ought td free themselves from responsibility by letting censure rest upon him. And, having censured, they ought to make the law of the land such that so deplorable a thing cannot occur again.

Did I understand the minister to say that there was a penalty upon the chief commissioner if he resigned in a pet, or, whether in a pet or not, suddenly, after large questions have been brought before him and leaving those questions undecided ? If he does this, he should lose part of his emoluments.
Mx\ FITZPATRICK. Taking the particular ease of the new chairman of the commission, the fact is that he must sit for ten years more in order to get the benefit of his whole retiring allowance. Up to this time, Mr. Killam has sat on the bench for twenty years, and, therefore, has acquired the right to a retiring, allowance of two-thirds of his present salary. His age, I believe, is fifty-five or something like that, and after he has held office for ten years longer, he will be able to retire with the full allowance that will be given him under this Act ?
Under section two he can retire at the end of fifteen years with an allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: An allowance of two-thirds-that is what I said.
This would be only ft partial disability then ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It means that he would not get the benefit of anything that would otherwise accrue' to him under this Act.

The Bill makes provision for a chairman who ' has become afflicted with a permanent infirmity disabling him from the due execution of his office.' In such a case, does he forfeit any of his emoluments ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. His position is that of a judge. If a judge is appointed to-day and to-morrow becomes afflicted with a permanent infirmity he is entitled to retire on an allowance of two-thirds' of his salary. Or if a judge occupies his position for fifteen years and then retires, he gets two-thirds of his salary. Or, if he keeps a place on the bench for thirty years, regardless of his age he is entitled to retire on his full salary. If he has attained the age of 75 years and has been twenty years on the bench or if he is 70 years of age and has been 25 years on the bench he may retire on full salary. So far as Sir. Killam is concerned he has acquired the right to retire with a pension of two-thirds of his salary-that right accrued to him when he had been fifteen years on the bench. But he must sit ten years more-because then he will only be sixty-five years of age, but will have had thirty years on the bench-in order to get his full retiring allowance. If he retires in the Interval, no matter what the cause-permanent disability or anything else-he does not receive his full retiring allowance.
Would bad temper be considered a permanent disability ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Some of us are infirm in that respect, 1 admit. But I hope that what happened before will never happen again. I think the penalty has been paid for what has occurred.

Does not the minister think there is some way of meeting the point ? Is it not fair that a judge put in this important position, having matters involving great interests to decide, should be precluded-unless he is disabled by the act of providence or something of that kind- from resigning until business before him has been disposed of, under penalty of forfeiting something Tie has already earned ? I have not learned what the practical situation is in this other case-whether there has been serious delay of important matters, or whether cases have to be gone over again at heavy expense. But, if that were the case we should provide against it occurring again, if we can. For, the minister will observe, there are two evils. In the first place there is the long delay of unfinished business-now nearly three
months-because of the sudden termination of the career of one of the commissioners. Then, on account of that sudden resignation, if the evidence has to be gone over again, there is a duplication of expense and a very serious loss. Is it not reasonable that there should be some provision in the Bill to prevent a man from leaving undecided the cases he has heard ? That it is reasonable is shown by what right my hon. friend (Sir Wilfred I.aurier) said- concerning .Tudge Killam himself. He told us that Judge Killam would not accept this office at once, not because he was not willing to take the office and receive the emoluments, but because he said considerations of duty prevented. Judge Killam said: Litigants have come before me and I have heard their evidence and must give decision in these cases. I cannot accept the invitation of the Prime Minister until I have finished that business. That was honourable. That is the basis upon which these things should be done. But if a man is not controlled by such considerations, then he should be controlled by compulsion or under penalty. The minister could add such a provision with perfect propriety and I think the country would approve it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under ordinary circumstances I should hate-that is I should much regret-being asked to make provision of that sort in connection with an office so important as this, an office to which we should appoint men of the highest possible honour-and that ought to be the best safeguard in cases of this sort. Still, I realize, in view of the experience we have had, that something of that kind should be considered. The difficulty was suggested by ,my hon. friend when the Bill was introduced. I have considered it and, have not abandoned the idea of meeting the difficulty. I have considered an amendment of the General Railway Act to meet some of the difficulties caused by the resignation of Mr. Blair. For instance, two members of the board travelled far and wide over the country and took evidence in important cases. These cases were not disposed of at the time of Mr. Blair's resignation, and it was my painful duty to advise the remaining commissioners that, quite clearly, they could not decide these cases, for the reason J:hat one of them had not heard the evidence. We are endeavouring to meet that difficulty with the co-operation of Justice KJilam by communicating with the parties and asking 'if they will give their consent to the disposition of the cases by the board as now constituted. My intention, I may say, is to move an amendment to the Act which will enable us to deal with such cases in the future. That is going as far as I have seen it right to go up to the present time. But I must confess that some amendment is needed, though I do not commit myself before having con-

suited my colleagues by promising to make a provision in the direction indicated by my Uon. friend ; but X will be glad of any assistance 1 can get in the direction of making it impossible that what has occurred may be repeated ; and before the Bill is read a third time I will ask for an adjournment in order to consider any suggestions I may receive from any quarter.

While my hon. friend is considering that, he must consider it doubly. There is the ordinary and general peccability and perverseness of human nature in the individual, an instance of which has been given in this case; but he must also remember that governments are liable to error; and the fact that such a state of things has arisen at all has been, in the first instance, because of lack of judgment in the appointing power, which is the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend does not expect I am going to introduce an amendment to correct that ?

Has the hon. gentleman thought of applying the remedy that I think used to exist in France, under a very ancient law, providing that the judges could not get their breakfast until they had rendered judgment ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid that would be too harsh.
On section 3,
Is there an age limit with respect to the commissioners ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, the Railway Act, section 8, provides the age limit for
commissioners at seventy-five years.
On section 4,

I have given notice to the Minister of Justice that upon the third reading of this Bill I propose to move that this clause be struck out. When the Bill was introduced I referred to this section, and gave some reasons why I thought it should not be left in the Bill. I do not propose to discuss the matter now, but merely to recall It to the attention of the minister, particularly in view of a good deal that has been said this afternoon.
On the preamble,

Before you proceed any further, I propose to add one or two clauses while we are in committee on this Bill. I move in amendment:
That section 3 of the Railway Act, 1903, is hereby amended by inserting after the word ' persons ' in the first line, the words ' and express companies.'
Section 3 reads :
This Act shall apply to all persons, companies and railways (other than government railways) within the legislative authority of the parlia-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
ment of Canada, and shall be incorporated and construed as one Act, with the Special Act, subject as herein provided.
In substance, I propose an amendment that has already been before the House in previous sessions, namely, that express companies shall come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. I am not going to take up the time of the House. I have often pointed out before that express companies are now doing more and more freight busirfess in this country, and their rates are not at present under the jurisdiction of this commission. I think they ought to be. Every one admits it. They are carrying more and more the freight of the country, they are carrying more and 'more a class of freight that needs to be handled quickly, and they are entitled to better terms for that. But as a matter of fact, all these express companies are the railway companies. They are owned and controlled by railway companies, the railway companies consider them as assets; and, as I pointed out, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in its annual report, calls the Dominion Express Company the property of its shareholders. These companies are doing more and more business, they charge now what they like. They are doing a freight business, they are owned by railways, and if the railways are to be regulated in their passenger rates and freight rates, they ought also to be regulated in their express charges. This same matter has come up at Washington the other day. A man of very large capital and engaged in some large industries in Michigan, went so far the other day as to petition Congress to take action which was in substance an impeachment of one of the members of the Senate. The charge which he made in substance was that the senator had acted in such a way as to entrench express companies so firmly that they could not be regulated in their charges and that all the railway interests were against any attempt at regulation. In fact, the entire business community of the United States is up in arms against the express charges in that country but so strong is the railway lobby in Washington that up to the present time they have not been regulated, they have not been brought under control and so strong is the express lobby backed up by the railway interests that the American government and the Postmaster General of that government are not in a position to establish a parcel post system like that which we have In this country and which they have in England and Germany. The Postmaster General of the United States himself is my authority for the statement that the express companies are so strong that they have prevented the adoption of a parcel post system. If we wish to regulate the express companies now is the time to regulate them. As an endorsement of what I have said to-day I would call the attention of the committee to the fact that boards of trade everywhere have asked

parliament to bring express companies within the jurisdiction of this Act.

It was stated last year that possibly this amendment would conflict with some other parts of the Act. I have no doubt that the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. F. Maclean) who introduced the amendment has considered that question, and it would probably be important to the committee to know whether it is a fact that it does not require a change in any other part of the Act to give it full effect. I have not myself looked into the question, but the objection was raised last year when this amendment was introduced. While I am on my feet I would say, in regard to what my hon. friend has said about the Postmaster General of the United States, that we have a very high authority in this House on that subject. Towards the close of last session, the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) called the attention of the House to the fact that we could not establish a free rural mail delivery in Canada, because in the United States the government had to yield to the demand of the mail carriers for increased wages, thus throwing the whole system out of working order. This wgs because the letter-carriers resorted to the carrying of parcels, thereby interfering with the express companies, and the express companies were enabled by their influence to bring such pressure to bear on the American government that the American government had to yield. This is in line with what my hon. friend has moved and it shows the enormous powers of these companies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The government has no opinion to express at this moment upon the merits of the amendment introduced by my hon. friend for South York (Mr. Maclean), but I have to observe to him that his amendment is premature and that he is out or order.
In what way ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because it is already before the House upon a Bill introduced by my hon. friend. My hon. friend's amendment is couched exactly in the same language as the Bill which he has introduced, which is Bill No. 4 on the order paper, and which is set down for its second reading to-day or whenever it is reached. Section 1 of the Bill reads as follows
Section 3 of the Railway Act, 1903, is hereby amended by inserting after the word ' persons ' in the first line the words ' and express companies.'
That is the first section of the Bill introduced by my hon. friend.
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And therefore it is out of order to move this section as an amendment to this Bill
In answer to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), I beg to say that the procedure which I am following to-day is the procedure which we followed last session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

I beg the right hon. gentleman's pardon. I moved these amendments in exactly the same way and no objection was taken then, I consented to my right hon. friend taking four days in the week for government business relying on my being able to discuss these amendments. The right hon. gentleman is in this matter departing from the practice of parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

Again I say that these amendments were brought up in this way last session and with the understanding that I would have an opportunity of moving them, I consented to the government taking four days in the week. Now, my right hon. friend may be able to close me | out, but I will ask the opinion not only of the chairman but of the House on this question. It is not going to facilitate the transaction of public business this session. I know what my right hon. friend wishes to do. He wishes to send me to the Railway Commission with my Bill. He brings in a new Bill of his own, we assist him all we can in getting his Bill through, but because I am a private member and he is the Prime Minster he has a law for himself, but he has not the same law for me. He may take refuge under a rule of order. I am going to sit down and let the chairman decide. I think I am quite in order and I hope the point will be discussed here before the ruling is given. Notwithstanding anything that is on the order paper, I say that when a public Bill is in committee it is the right and privilege of every hon. member, even if he is a private member, to make any amendment he sees fit to the Bill under consideration.

Before the point of order is decided I -would like to discuss the question. A private member introduces a Bill in which there are certain clauses, the government introduces another Bill, and although it may be necessary to make the latter Bill workable that it should be amended, because the Bill introduced by the private member includes a clause similar in terms to a proposed amendment, you preclude a private member from amending the government Bill. I am aware of the rule of the House which declares that where a member gives notice of motion and it is on the order paper he cannot move that motion or what is set forth in that motion as an amendment to a Bill. The proper thing to do under those circumstances is to j drop the motion, but I do not think that rule applies at all or that it can be held that

when a private member introduces a Bill he is precluded afterwards from moving any clause of that Bill as an amendment to a public Bill.

I would like to point out to my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) that if, when he gave notice to amend Bill No. 30, he had looked at section 3, he would have found that the language he was using in the resolution would not apply to the section because he proposes to amend it by adding these words ' and express companies.' It was not necessary for the hon. gentleman to do that. All that he was required to give notice of was the word ' express.' Therefore, he would have got over the difficulty if he had paid attention to the wording and the objection raised by the right hon. leader of the government, would not apply to this case as I am afraid it does apply on account of my hon. friend having introduced his Bill first, as the right hon. leader of the government has said, and then having moved a resolution covering exactly the same thing afterwards.

I hold that we have followed this practice for many years. It is a common thing in this House to have two or three Bills standing as amendments to the election law, when the government move to bring in a Bill and ask that the Bills introduced by private members be allowed to stand as they will incorporate the clauses contained in these Bills in the government measure. Although there is a rule which says that you shall not' anticipate what is on the order paper we do anticipate it by incorporating some of the clauses contained in these Bills, and when we have reached these Bills afterwards they have been allowed to drop. We have done that several times. All that my hon. friend would require to do, when he reaches his own Bill, is to say: I have incorporated the provisions that I intend to enact in this Bill, in an amendment to the Railway Act which you propose as a government measure, you have allowed me to do the same thing with Bills before and I am endeavouring to do it today.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would in the
first place answer m.v hon. friend from Elgin (Mr. Ingram) that the resolutions which he has addressed to the House have no bearing upon this occasion. My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) gave notice of his amendment, but he required no notice of an amendment to a public Bill. Notice of amendments is required only in the case of private Bills and he could at the table offer an amendment to a public Billl if it affected ihe Bill. Therefore, the question is not affected one way or the other by the notice. The amendment which he offers to the House is simply that we shall take the first section of bis Bill and introduce it as an amendment in the present Bill. My hon. friend has been very candid as to why he acts in this man-Mr. HAGGART.
ner. He has a Bill before the House and he can move it; he has let the opportunity of moving it pass three or four times, to my knowledge, and why would he not move it ? Because the policy of my hon. friend is different from the policy of the government. I told him-it is on the record-when the Bill was first brought to the attention of the House that we had no opinion to offer upon it; we were not prepared to say yes or no. There is a good deal in the proposition he makes that express companies should be committed to the jurisdiction of the commission, but we informed my hon. friend that it was not our intention to take up this matter in the House; we wanted to refer it to the Railway Commission, there to be dealt with and discussed in the light of full information obtained from all parties interested in it. But this policy does not suit the convenience of my hon. friend.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He will not have it this way and, therefore, because our views do not accord with his views, he will not accept the very reasonable offer which we made to him of referring this matter to the Railway Commission; he wants to get his Bill passed by a side wind, and he wants to bring it to the attention of the House in spite of the rules of the House. My hon. friend has no need of taking refuge and of crying misericordia because he is a private member; He has as much right as a minister to introduce legislation; he has availed himself of this right, but because the Bill we introduce does not suit him he wants to violate the rules of the House in order to offer his amendment to the House at this moment.
Will the hon. gentleman quote the rule ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is much
latitude for amending. Any amendment may be brought in that has reference to the matter under discussion, but the rule is that if an amendment, which it is sought to introduce to the Bill before the House is already a notice for consideration on another proceeding, that amendment is therefore out of order. There is no doubt about that; every one knows it ; but my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has offered a most subtle distinction and it is this : That the rule will apply to a motion but not to a Bill.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Where do you get that?
I would say

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Allow me. It
has no bearing, it is all technicality and no substance. There is no proceeding before the House which can be initiated, whether it be a Bill or anything else, except upon a motion. The Bill of my hon. friend, Bill

No. 4, stands upon the order paper in this way :
Second reading of Bill (No. 4), an Act to amend the Railway Act.
When the Speaker comes to call this order he will put the question to the House and my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) will move for the second reading of this Bill. Therefore, it is not necessary at all to say that this rule applies to a motion and not to a Bill. Every Bill must be introduced by a motion and it would be, I think, the most extraordinary proceeding that a rule of that kind should apply when there is a motion and should not apply when it is a Bill under discussion. What is the essence and the object of this rule? It is simply to ensure that a matter which is before the House cannot be taken from its order as a substitute for another order. That is the ruling given by previous speakers. Bourinot, at page 442, note (i) says :
It is not regular to move as an amendment to a question a motion of which notice has been given-and when it appears on the notice paper in a particular place.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Speaker Oui-met decided in 1889 (Journals, page 214):
It is not in .accordance with the rules or parliamentary usage to take a motion out of its proper place, and move it as an amendment to another question.
Is it more in accordance with the usage of parliament to take a Bill out of its proper place ? To say that you cannot take a motion out of its place, but you can a Bill, is not sense, or I might use even stronger language. My hon. friend will have to exercise a good deal of reasoning in order to satisfy the House of the extraordinary proposition that a motion cannot be taken out of its order and a Bill can.
Then, May, which is a standard work on the principles of procedure, says :
Nor can an amendment he moved which anticipates a motion or amendment of which notice has been given on matters contained ia the order of the day.
So, therefore, I submit, Mr. Chairman, that according to the principles of parliamentary usage this amendment is out of order.

In this case there has been no notice of motion given. My hon. friend proposes to amend a public Bill. The argument of the right hon. the Prime Minister is that this is virtually a Bill moved as an amendment to a public Bill. The rule of the House is clear, that no Bill can be moved out of its proper order. Is this the moving of a Bill out of its proper order ? The other rule which applies to motions something similar to this is that no motion of which notice has been given shall be moved in amendment to a public Bill, nor shall the substance of any motion. Does this come under either
category? Not at all. Look at the absurdity of the position. A private member or half a dozen private members may give notice of Bills proposed, say on election matters or on a dozen other questions, and they may intend to move them. Then, according to the argument that has been advanced, because one of them has a clause in it referring to a particular election matter, it would not be competent for another member to move a similar motion in amendment to a government Bill, because some member or perhaps half a dozen members in the House had introduced Bills along the same lines.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Why certainly.

The object of the rule is to prevent a motion or a Bill being by any means or in any form moved out of its proper order in order that the House should discuss it. The other reason is that when a party gives a notice of motion that the motion should be on the order paper of the House, and that he should have an opportunity of discussing that measure, and that no other member of the House, by a side wind or an amendment to a public Bill, should take the credit of the motion whicn some hon. gentleman has moved. I contend, Mr. Chairman, that this does not come within either of these categories; this is a clause in a Bill which my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) has introduced. He is moving it in amendment to a public Rill but that does not necessarily mean that it is the introduction of a Bill out of its ordinary course on the order paper.

There may be a difference of opinion as to the rule of parliament in connection with this matter. I think the first minister was not present when this Bill was introduced on the 9th day of this month. At that time a certain understanding was come to between the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) and the hon. the Minister of Justice in reference to the discussion of this Bill. The discussion is thus reported in 'Hansard.'
Bill (No. 36) to amend the Railway Act, 1903-* Mr. Fitzpatrick-read the second time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When shall the House go into committee ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What my hon. friend really wishes, I presume, is to move, by way of amendment, the different clauses of the Bill now in his name on the order paper.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it would be advisable to thresh them out in committee. There are some features in one of the clauses of his Bill which I think ought to be discussed.
