I am not quite ready to go on now, but will be on Tuesday.
That seems to me to be a sort of understanding between the Minister of Justice

and the hon. member for South York. Therefore, I think the hon. gentleman is fairly entitled to discuss his Bill now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is very kind indeed to champion the cause of my hon. friend from South York. If the hon. member for South York has had any understanding with me, I am quite sure he can state it himself, and I am willing to abide by it.

If the hon. Minister of Justice asks me to explain, I will say that I understood that I might bring up the substance of my Bill in connection with his Bill to amend the Railway Act. I think we had that understanding, and I leave the Minister of Justice to say whether or not that is the case. Of course, that is quite outside of the question of order. I do not care how it is settled. I wish to see the rules of parliament observed ; but last session we proceeded in this way, and no objection was taken, and for that reason I consented, as I might not otherwise have done, to the proposal to take four days of the week for government measures.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What my hon. friend from South York has said with respect to the understanding is absolutely correct, and I certainly was under the impression at the time he made the suggestion that he might move in committee. I was ignorant of the rule referred to by the Prime Minister. I do not want to break the rule of parliament, but I am sure that the Prime Minister will agree with me, that if the rule is such that the hon. member for South York cannot move now, a day ought to be fixed on which he could bring up his Bill for discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I certainly did not confer with the Minister of Justice before I raised this point. I did not know of the understanding between the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for South York, or I would not have raised it. I will not press the point.

If I recollect aright, there have been many Bills in the same position, and no objection has been raised before. We followed the course proposed with regard to the Franchise law, the Election law and the Alien Labour law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend forgets that there is a difference between this occasion and the occasions to which he refers. On those occasions the government accepted the amendments, and the moment that was done, there was no question of order. But when a Bill of this kind is proposed, which the government does not accept, we have a right to invoke the rule.

I think that is a strange argument-that one rule is to apply to the | government and another to private mem- | bers. I thought parliamentary rules were Mr. INGRAM.
to apply to the government and to private members alike ; but the Prime Minister has given an entirely different turn to them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not at all. If, when a government Bill is under consideration, amendments are moved and the government accepts them, no point is raised on either side ; but if the government or any one else objects, the rule applies.

That was not the case. Those Bills were on the order paper, and it was suggested that they could be better included in government Bills than passed as separate Bills. When the Railway Act was under discussion some of those Bills were incorporated in it. That was done because it was the usual practice that had applied, not only to railway Bills, but to many others. Several times we held Bills over so that a portion of them might be incorporated in some government Bill.

I approach this question with a good deal of diffidence, I confess, because I have become somewhat rusty in my parliamentary law ; but I think the right hon. leader of the government is correct in his interpretation of the rule. A Bill starring on the order paper is really notice of a motion, and it seems to me that the rule that applies to motions would apply with equal force to public Bills. But there have been instances, and many instances, both under the present administration and under their predecessors, in which a public Bill introduced by a private member, or some of its provisions, have so commended themselves to the government that the government has been quite ready to accept them. The member who has introduced the Bill is advised by the government that they will accept either the whole Bill or certain portions of it; and when the Bill is reached on the order paper, it is either dropped or the member who has introduced it moves that the order be discharged, and the Bill is taken up as an amendment to a Bill of a similar character introduced by the government. My own opinion is that the right hon. leader of the government is correct in his interpretation of the rule ; but as there seems to have been an understanding between the hon. Minister of Justice and my hon. friend from South York, I am sure that the government will carry out that understanding and allow my hon. friend from South York to proceed with his amendments when this Bill comes up at a future stage, if not at the present sitting.

Notwithstanding the statement of my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. 'White), I must say that I entirely differ from him. A Bill is not a motion. Motions have often been dropped,
* because their being on the order paper prevented members moving them as amendments to Bills. My hon. friend suggests

that because of an agreement made between the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. member for South York, we can set aside all the rules of the House. That is an anomalous position. It is only by the unanimous consent of the House that a rule can be set aside. I have been in the House a long while, and I have never before heard the rule in question applied to a Bill. I have heard it applied to motions hundreds of times, and I have seen the motions dropped in order that the members making such motions might be in a position to move amendments to Bills. But while we live we learn, and I learn now for the first time that this principle applies, not only to motions, but to Bills.

I feel that I ought to defer to the superior knowledge of my hon. friend from South Lanark ; but I frankly confess that when I had the honour of occupying the position of the Speaker of the House of Commons my hon. friend from South Lanark CMr. Haggart) and myself differed upon points of order very frequently. Not only he but the other members of the government, of which he was so distinguished an ornament at that time, also differed from me with regard to points of order and procedure. I had up to that time given considerable study to those subjects, and I do not think it is quite within the province of my hon. friend from South Lanark to say that I ever assumed that because there happened to be an agreement similar to that in the present instance between the Minister of Justice and the hon. minister for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean), namely, that this question should be taken up when the Railway Bill was being considered, such an agreement can set aside the rules of this parliament. I do not believe it can. I do not think the rules of parliament can be set aside by any such agreement, but If the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for South York did come to the agreement in question, it seems to me that the government ought, in all fairness to the hon. gentleman, to agree to the proposition he makes, and have the matter he has brought up discussed when this Railway Bill is before the House either at this or some future stage.

While I agree in the opinions expressed by my grave and reverend co-members, I wish to say-and I would ask the Prime Minister to make a note of it-that when we are revising the rules of the House-and it is high time that we did-we should make provision that the same procedure ought to apply to public Bills as to government Bills. If a private member's Bill has to go to the Railway Committee so also should a government Bill. It is because there is a different procedure applied to public Bills than is applied to government Bills that I have to resort to parliamentary strategy and try to get my proposals discussed in connection with those of the government. The rule ought to be that exactly the same kind of treatment should be accorded to all amendments to the Railway Act. If that is not to be the case, and if I were introducing a Bill again to amend the Railway Act, I would simply put in one clause, a non-important clause, and keep my other ammunition in my pocket until the government Bill to amend the Act came up.

As far as I can judge, the point of order raised by the right hon. the first minister is well taken. From my reading of the rule, I think there can be no two opinions about it. I think we had better not depart from the good healthy practice of sticking closely to the rules of this House. We do not know where a matter of this kind may end. I do not see how this House can be called upon to recognize any agreement made between two individual members which is not known to every member. My position is this, I intend to vote for this amendment, whether it comes up as an amendment to the Railway Act or a portion of the Bill of the hon. member for York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). It makes no difference, so far as my position is concerned, whether I vote to-day on this proposition as an amendment to the government Bill, or on some other day, when it comes before the House in the form of a Bill; but I do think we had better stand by the rules of the House and not have it said that one hon. member must have one rule applied to him and another hon. member have the benefit of a different rule. Possibly in a very short time I may be ruled out of order on the very point now raised. Why should I not have the same privilege as my hon. friend from York ? I feel strongly that we should adhere to the rules of the House, and I desire to make it plain that, so far as my position is concerned, I intend to vote for this amendment regarding express companies, whether it comes in the form of an amendment to this Bill or of the Bill placed on the notice paper by the hon. member for York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) I understand the right l-.on. first minister has withdrawn his point of order, and now it is open to any other member to raise the same point, and I desire to do so. I submit to you, Sir, that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York is out of order.

After the declaration of the hon. member for Halton, (Mr. Henderson) I withdraw any claim to any privilege arising out of any understanding and I leave the hon. gentleman to shoulder tlie responsibility. You can report the Bill, Mr. Speaker.

As the government have taken two more of the days belonging to private members, it may be utterly impossible for this Bill to come before the House unless brought up in connection with some government Bill, and my hon. friend will be de-

prived of the right to have his Bill dealt with.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend from York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has had many opportunities of moving his Bill.
I agree to that.
I understand that he could not go on for want of certain information which he desired to have when discussing it.
That is right.

Then the government took the private members day away. In other sessions, when that happens, it is usual to draw attention to the fact that certain important Bills are on the order paper and permission is given td the member to bring his Bill before the House and have it dealt with, if not as a separate Bill, in connection with some government measure. We have done that frequently in connection with railway charters and the labour question and various other questions without objection ; and if we abandon that privilege to-day, we are giving up a privilege of our own, and our privileges are quite as important to us as the rules that govern us.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A good deal of time has been wasted in discussing a matter which was settled some time ago. This Bill has been called several times. Sometimes it was postponed to suit the convenience of my hon. friend and other times to suit mine. It was understood between us that when the government Bill reached the committee stage, we would consider my hon. friend's amendments. But as regards the practice referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) he is entirely in error. I have had more to do with these Bills than he has-if he will pardon me for saying so- and my invariable practice is, when I am introducing general legislation, to adopt any principle that I find in a Bill that stands in the name of any private member on the order paper. I adopt the principle of such a Bill of my own motion, just as I would have a right to amend my own Bill. But I cannot do that in this instance. If I felt free to adopt the principle of my hon. friend's Bill and add it as an amendment to my own. I would do so. But I intend to oppose his amendment and give reasons why the House should not adopt it.
Perhaps it would be possible to suggest a compromise that would satisfy both sides

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To go on with our business would satisfy me perfectly.

That is just the suggestion -that I was going to make. Suppose the hon. gentleman is allowed to proceed with his Bill ; and, then in view of the number of new 'members in the House who have not heard the matter discussed, we could Mr. SPROULE.
refer it to the Railway Committee, with a view to having all interests heard and the matter fully discussed.

I appreciate very much what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) has said; and what he has said is exactly correct. But I do not wish to appear as taking advantage of any rule of the House. Nor do I wish to be heard in this discussion merely as a matter of courtesy. I thought I was within my right. But, of course, I defer to what has been said. Another opportunity will be afforded me to bring this measure up

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Next Monday.

Yes, it will come up next Monday, and there will be an opportunity for discussion. All I had in mind was to facilitate the public business and help to make the session as short as possible. In view of the scrupulous consideration of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) for the rules of order, I must go about it in another way.

There is no difficulty in getting over the point raised by the hon. member from Halton (Mr. Henderson). If my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) desires to have his Bill discharged from the order paper. When it comes up for discussion he can do that and then he will be at perfect liberty to proceed with his amendment. The fact is, he wants to have two strings to his bow-he wants to move in committee, and, if defeated in committee he wants to take up his Bill. I think that would be contrary to all the rules of parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is what is called strategy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must rule the point of order well taken according to rule 24, which says :
All items standing on the orders of the day shall be taken up according to the precedence assigned to each on the order book ;-
But there is a reservation made for government measures.
The right being reserved to the administration of placing government orders at the head of the list in the rotation in which they are to be taken on the days on which government Bills have precedence.
I	find this amendment is identical word for word with Bill No. 4 which stands on the order paper as a public Bill.
Bill reported.
Rt. Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

['The Minister of Justice will move some Bills standing in his name, and then we shall go into supply. I understand the Minister of Inland Revenue will be prepared to proceed. If his estimates are completed, the Minister of Agriculture will take up some of his items, and, if these are finished, the Minister of Public Works will go on.']

Will the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) permit me to call his attention to a statement made by him yesterday in reply to a question by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), who is not here to-day, on the subject of the elections in Manitoba :
I may inform my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) that I received to-day two memoranda from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery on this subject, hut I have not yet been able to look at them. I will be able to give him an answer io-n.orrow.
That ' to-morrow ' is to-day. Can the right hon. gentleman give us any information on the subject now ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to say that the matter will have to stand over until to-morrow, because I could not look into it.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Public buildings-Manitoba-Brandon drill hall, $20,000.
['I am sorry to say that the matter will have to stand over until to-morrow, because I could not look into it.']
No expenditure has been made on that yet. There is one squadron of mounted rifles there.

What is the cost of building a drill hall such as is proposed to be erected in Brandon ? What would be about the difference in cost between erecting this building and a building of the same size in Ontario ?
The architect thinks there might be a difference of 10 per cent greater in Manitoba.
What is the material used ?
It will be a wooden building with brick veneer.

I was surprised when I was out there in some of those far western towns to find out how cheaply brick are produced. At Edmonton they produce brick for 35 a thousand, at Moosejaw for about $8. I think we pay more than that in the city of Toronto, or quite as much. Of course, bricks can be made cheaper at Edmonton, because coal Is more easily procured. It seems to me that with brick so cheap in the west it would be cheaper in the long run to make the building of brick than of timber. or even of timber with brick veneering.
The minister said it would cost 10 per cent more to build in Manitoba ; but if bricks are so cheap there, where does the extra 10 per cent come from ?
There is a considerable difference In the price of labour and of other materials than brick.

I desire to bring to the attention of the minister the urgent necessity that exists for a drill hall in the town of Minnedosa. I think Minnedosa has got the largest company of any of the small places in the province of Manitoba, and in the drill contest in Brandon last year they carried off the major portion of the honours. Virden is a smaller town than Minnedosa. They make bricks in Minnedosa, and I would urge the claims of that town on the minister in fulfilment of the promise that was made last year.

I will bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Militia.
Dominion buildings-Manitoba-renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $8,000,
Wrho is the inspector for Dominion buildings now in Manitoba ?

Mr. Chisholm.
t
There is an increase of $2,000 over last year ; why is that ?

There is a larger number of buildings.
Selkirk public building, $15,000.

No site has been purchased yet. The building will accommodate customs, post office, Indian affairs and fisheries. The population at the last census was 2,188. Customs and postal revenues amounted last year to between $5,000 and $6,000. In order to accommodate these four offices I do not think we can put up a building there at a less cost than $16,000.
Virden drill hall, $20,000.
What is the size of that building ?
60 feet 10 inches by 31 feet 8 inches.
What is it constructed of ?
It is brick veneer.
Had you to pay for the site ?
The site was given free.
When is it to be completed ?
In October of this year.
What is the total cost ?
The estimated total cost is $15,000.
Then what are you asking $20,000 for ?

I see that I have a memorandum in connection with this vote
/



which I was not aware of. I move that the vote be reduced to $15,000.
Motion agreed to.

['I see that I have a memorandum in connection with this vote
/', '

which I was not aware of. I move that the vote be reduced to $15,000.']
Who has the contract ?

Mr. W. H. Ireland.
Winnipeg district military stores building,
That was explained last night.
Is that the general system adopted all over the country ?

Yes, at the different headquarters.
Winnipeg-new immigration building, $62,000.

This is to provide for the completion of the building being erected at the request of the Department of the Interior. A contract has been let to the Manitoba Construction Company. The building is to be completed by the first of April, 1905. The total estimated cost is $177,000.
iMr. STAPLES. Where is this building to be located ?

The building is located on a site transferred from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company situated between Maple and Fonseca streets, and has an area of 200 feet by 61 feet 4 inches. The contract for the building is $162,000 and the total cost will be about $177,000.
Has there been any change since last year ?
Yes, the building has been made fire proof and increased in size.
It was estimated last year at $60,000.
Who has the contract ?
The Manitoba Construction Company.
Is that building in charge of the engineer located at Winnipeg or is there a superintendent for this work ?
No, it is under the supervision of the architect Mr. Joseph Chisholm.
A permanent officer ?

Yes.
Winnipeg military buildings-quarters for non-commissioned officers, including guard room, &c., $6,000.
Nothing has been spent on that ?

No, there has been no money spent on that. This is supposed to be quarters for the married non-commis-Mr. HYMAN.
sioned officers of ' A' squadron, guard room, cells, quartermaster's stores, lecture room, &c.
Is this connected with the armoury ?
No, this is for the permanent force.
Has the hon. minister in his department a list of the military properties taken over from the imperial authorities by the colonial authorities ?

That will be in the Militia Department.
Winnipeg new post office-land and building. $300,000.
What was the cost of the site ?

The site cost $132,350.
IMr. W. J. ROCHE. What is the estimated total cost of the building ?
Including the site ?
No, outside of the site.
The estimate is increased a great deal from that of last year.
Of course, the estimate was given before the contract was made.
Who recommended the site 1
I do not know7, I am sure. This was very fully discussed last year in the House. It was a very profitable bargain. We could have sold the site any time for more money.
Is it a corner lot ?
No, it is not a corner lot. There will be space on both sides of the building.
What is going to be done with the old post office ?
The idea is to use the old post office building for a customs house.

There was a question raised last year by the hon. gentleman who represented Provencher in regard to the title of the old Bannatyne property which contained the stipulation that the site was only to be used for the post office building. He stated that the site was given for a small consideration on the understanding that it was to be used for a post office building. The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sutherland) stated that the matter had only been brought to his attention the previous day in regard to the title and that he w7ould inquire into it. I do not think he ever furnished the House with any information on the subject. Was

there not some distinct understanding that that site was to be used for all time to come as a post office site Y

The deputy informs me that the matter was looked into both before and after it was mentioned iu the House and that there is no evidence in the department of any kind on which such a statement can be based.

X will just read what the hon. minister said last year.
The matter of the title to the site of the post office in Winnipeg was brought to my attention only yesterday. I am having it investigated. I believe there is some condition, but X do not think it is so narrow as that mentioned by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. LariviSre), -that the site is to be occupied by the post office. I believe that the land was sold on the condition that it was to be used as a site for government offices.
IMr. HYMAN. Well, these are government officers.
So he must have had some evidence in his possession when he was able to make that statement.
I will ask the deputy to look into the matter.
What Is the size of the site ?
The site is of an irregular shape, 166 feet front by 80 feet in one part and 134 feet in another part.
From whom was it purchased ?
Alloway and J. W. Good.
Is that not a very good price, $132,000 ?

That is the price. The information I received from the department is that the property could be sold to-day for more money. I know that the department has been looking for some more land there, and it is almost impossible to get any more land near the centre of the city for anything like what we would consider a moderate cost.
Who negotiated the sale 1
Thos. B. Metcalfe.
Did he receive any commission ?

There has been no expenditure other than the cost of the site.
Public buildings, Northwest Territories-barracks for permanent corps, Strathcona Horse, $40,000.
Where is that barracks ?

There has been no decision by the Militia Department yet as to the
headquarters of the Strathcona corps, and therefore the matter is in that shape. This is for the permanent corps.
Calgary public buildings-enlargement of post office and examining warehouses, changes, fittings, &c., $40,000.

This building is being enlarged for the use of these different departments. The building has become altogether too small and it is being enlarged. The area of the present post office is 1,360 feet. With this addition there will be nearly three times that amount of area.
Calgary land titles office, $15,000.
,T. ROCHE. Would the minister make an explanation ?

I think I shall ask to have that item stand.
Item allowed to stand.
Court House,-lock-up and police accommodation. $1,500.

This is to provide accommodation at different places.
Edmonton jail, $33,000.
This is for the continuation of the work on the jail there. It has been in progress for some time.
What is the total cost ?

The contract Is for ^50,150.
Medicine Hat, public building, $15,000.

This is to provide a public building at Medicine Hat. The postal revenue is $4,679 and the customs duties $20,113.
Moosejaw public building, $20,000.
What is that ?
That is for the purpose of a public building at Moosejaw. It is under contract. The postal revenue in the year 1903-4 was $7,800 and the customs revenue $49,700.
What are you building there ?
A brick building with stone foundation.
Can your officer tell you what he has to pay for brick there ?

Of course it is let by tender, but he thinks the price is between seven and eight dollars a thousand.
Prince Albert, public building, $40,000.
That is under contract.
How much is that to cost ?
What is the population of Prince Albert ?
The population is about 2,300 now, but this is for a court house, post office, customs house, land office and registry office.
And what is the revenue there ?
The postal revenue is $5,249 and the customs revenue $8,427.
What public buildings have they now ?
Nothing but an old court house and jail. They use an old one-story building for a land office.
How much was paid for this site ?
Then the building is not to be on the site of the old court house ?
No.
Why ?
The old court house, I am informed, is quite out of the town.

That might have been said when the town consisted of one street along the river ; then it was a couple of streets back, but there is a nice residental district growing up near the post office. A gentleman who is now in the Senate lives farther out than the court house.
When will that be completed ?

The contract was let on January 1, and the building will be completed in October, 1906.
Red Deer court house, land office and lock-up,
That is under contract.
What is that to cost ?

The total cost is estimated to be $20,000.
Mr. FOSTER, When is it to be finished?
On November 20.

Well, it is a nice little town, and that is not too expensive a building for it.
Regina post office, custom house, &c., $20,000.
The postal revenue of Regina last year was $20,736 and the customs revenue, $241,000. I estimate that, Regina being the capital, the building will cost complete,. $55,000.
Where is it to be placed ?
No site has yet been purchased.
Have there been any negotiations?
There have been some negotiations, but no site has been selected.

I -would like to ask the hon. minister what the policy of the government is in regard to some of these estimates. We have voted this evening, and are no doubt going to be called on to vote again, sums of money which are destined to be expended for purely provincial works in the North-, west, such as jails and asylums. The Autonomy Bill, as it is called, will come into force on July 1 next, and what will then become of these votes? Some of them may not have been expended; some of the buildings are in course of construction, and some may not be commenced before July 1. What course does the government intend to take with regard to those works which are provincial in their nature? Because once parliament has voted an item, even for a work of a purely provincial nature, it cannot very well be varied. Parliament having voted a specific sum for a specific purpose, it must be spent for that purpose and for no other.

In any ease, we have to carry out our contracts, and these votes are for contracts which were entered into by the Public Works Department some time ago. I do not know that the government have arrived at any conclusion, but after the Northwest Government Bill passes, there is no doubt that all the buildings intended for purely provincial purposes will be transferred to the provinces. The only difficulty will be as to joint buildings, which are used partly for provincial purposes and partly for Dominion purposes, such as the Prince Albert building, which is used as a post office and custom house and also as a court house. In such cases we shall either have to take over the building and make some financial allowance to the provincial government or they will take over the building and make some financial allowance to us. I do not see any other way in which we can do what is fair and right.
Has the government considered the question of a penitentiary for the Territories?
I do not know that the matter has been under consideration. I believe the Edmonton jail has been suggested for that purpose.

As some of these votes are for works of a purely provincial character,
1 think it would be advisable not to vote too large an amount for these purposes.

I am not going to ask for any new votes for works of that character. We are only providing for contracts \vhich have already been entered into.
Saskatoon public building, $5,000.

The postal revenue in the year 1902-3 was $2,000 and in the year 1903-4

,$4,195. Saskatoon is quite a growing town. The building is estimated to cost $9,500, and the total cost, including heating, contingencies, &c., at $14,500. The work is not yet commenced. The building will be of brick.
What is the population of the town?
I have not the present population. In 1901 it was between 500 and 600.

Saskatoon is a very nice place. It has derived its importance largely from the fact that during the last couple of years it has been the point where settlers coming in by the Regina, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway leave the railway and start to tramp to their destination. In a short time both the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern will have lines through Saskatoon, and it will then be an important town.
British Columbia-renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., to Dominion buildings, $8,000.

I would like to ask the government if it has any intention to put up a public building in the town of Pinclier Creek ? We have never had a public building in that town, not even one in which to hold the court, and I think it has g population which fairly entitles it to a building such as those which have been erected in many other towns not so large and not increasing in importance so rapidly.

I would remind my hon. friend that if a public building is required there for the purposes of a court house, after the 1st of July it will be the duty of the new provincial government to take that matter in hand, and my hon. friend will have to make his representations to the provincial authorities. I am not aware of any representations having been made for the purpose of having this government erect a public building there, but am always glad to hear any my hon. friend has to make.
Ferule, B.C., public building, $10,000.
The postal revenue is $5,500 ; the customs, $8,200. It is estimated the building will cost $21,500. The site has not been selected yet.
Is there any difficulty about the location of the site ?

I do not know of any.
New Westminster public building-enlargement for accommodation of Indian branch, $7,-
000.

This is asked for the purpose of putting up a building for the Interior Department ; but since this vote has been placed in the estimates, I have had my attention called frequently to the overcrowding in the New Westminster building at present. The fishery branch of the Marine and Fisheries service may be put into that new building, which will add to its cost. The $7,000 is only intended to cover a building for the Interior Department.
Vancouver public building, $100,000.

This is not only to be a post office. It is intended for a post office, custom house and examining warehouse. The plans and specifications are being prepared. It is going to be very expensive. I do not see how that building can be put up at a less cost than $400,000 to $450,000.
When will it be completed ?

As the contract has not been made yet, I am unable to say, but it will be completed as soon as possible, because there is great need for it at present.
Salaries to resident clerks of works, assistants, &c., public buildings, generally, $14,000.
This is to pay the salaries of the clerks of works and their assistants in other places than Ottawa.
How many are paid out of this $14,000 ?
Ten.
They are distributed all over, are they not ?
Yes.
Can the hon. minister give the distribution ?
There are two in Ottawa, one in Quebec, one in Winnipeg, two in Montreal, two in Victoria, one in Regina, one in Three Rivers.
Are there any in New Brunswick ?
Yes.
Any in Nova Scotia ?
Our work is done there by Mr. Doddrell, engineer of the department.
These are all the clerks of works employed in superintending public buildings throughout the Dominion ?
Yes.
That does not mean architects ?
No.
I did not notice that you read over any for Ontario.
Mr. Curry, the architect in Toronto, does our work there.

I suppose the hon. gentleman is continuing the system that has existed for years. Where there is a public work erected, you employ a superintendent of works at so much per day. That system has been continued for years, and every session it is objected to. These men simply

assist in prolonging the work by not insisting on more men being put on the building. You pay them from $2.50 to $7 per day, and the longer the building is under construction the better for them, consequently you will have a building take two years in construction which an ordinary contractor would build in four or five months.

Surely, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) has overstated the case. The contract for the construction of the building fixes a time within which it is to be finished. You must have a clerk of works, somebody who will represent the department in the work. We cannot employ architects all the time to do that work. In cities, for instance, in London or in Toronto, we employ an architect to overlook work of this kind. But, there are places where public buildings are under construction and where there are no architects. We must, in such cases, have a clerk of works, and I can hardly conceive of any way to pay him except by the day. You could hardly give him so much for the work
Why not?
Well it would practically come down to so much a day anyhow.

You could pay such an officer percentage on the contract price. If that were done, he would have an interest in earning his money as quickly as possible, and he would insist on the proper number of men being on the job. On the other hand, if he is paid $5 or $7 a day, he' will be very glad to have the time of construction an extended one. We suffer loss year in and year out in this way.

I have done a considerable amount of building and I never heard of the inspectors being paid on any such a plan as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) speaks of. I do not think that plan is followed by private individuals or companies. As I say, we employ an architect where wre can, but in the case of a building being put up in a small town, it is impossible to employ an architect.

It is not necessary that a man should be an architect to be able to insist that the contractor shall carry on his work according to the plans and specifications, and shall put on enough men to finish the work in a reasonable time. In my own city, a building was erected by the municipality costing $50,000 or $60,000. The architect in charge was paid on the percentage plan, and he insisted on a proper number of men being employed. But he was inspector also of the government armoury building. He inspected the armoury building in the morning and the municipal building for the balance of the day. He could stand it to have only two or three men on the armoury, but he insisted on the full number of men on the municipal building. The result was Mr. INGRAM.
that the municipal building was completed more quickly than the armoury was, which cost only about half as much. When you consider the number of buildings being constructed in the Dominion, you will see, that, in the aggregate this is a serious grievance. With private individuals it is by no means unusual to pay architects on the percentage plan. It is a common plan in all our cities.

I would call the minister's attention to a case of this description. The building was under contract, and the inspector was appointed to overseethe work, I presume at a salary of about $J a day. The unfortunate part of it was that this inspector was not a mechanic of any description. The building was about a year and a half under construction, and the inspector received $1,200 or $1,300 for his services.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Herron) tell me to which case he refers.

Yes, the court house at Fort Macleod. I do not think the inspector in that case had enough mechanical knowledge to superintend the building of a pumphouse to say nothing of a court house. Yet he drew a salary during construction.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Herron) is mistaken in his facts. In the case to which he refers the inspector was paid $4 a day not $7.
Will the hon. minister tell us what the inspector received altogether? My information is that he drew about $1,300.
What the minister says does not lessen the fact that inspectors are paid $7 a day in British Columbia.
Take one of these clerks of works as an example-take the one at Quebec. He is paid by the year, his salary being $1,282. Just what does he do? What are his duties from January to December ?
He practically has charge of all the government works in that vicinity.
What does the hon. minister mean by saying that he ' has charge ' of these works?

He looks after all the buildings, sees that the caretakers do their work. In this particular case, the inspector has charge of the public buildings at Grosse lie, and he has to go there very often. It is the duty of these inspectors to have charge of the public buildings in their districts.

Is his district the whole province?
Mi-. HYMAN. No, we have an inspector in Montreal.

This inspector is for ivhat is called the Quebec district. He has to go

to places where there are public buildings and make an inspection of those buildings.

He goes where we send him. We use these officers largely in the purchase of sites. No site is purchased by the department without a report either from an officer sent from the department or from one of these so-called inspectors.
When the government wants a site the inspector reports upon it? That is one thing he does. Does he oversee buildings under construction?
He supervises all the work of repairs and renewals-not necessarily new buildings, because in that case he would have to be on the new building all the time.
He has nothing to do with the new buildings?

That is all arranged by the architect. If, in any particular instance we can use one of these officers, we do so. For instance, in the post office building in Ottawa, the work is overseen by Mr. Adams who is paid out of this vote.

He is in Ottawa, and has nothing else to do, and so he is there. But in the case of this clerk of works in Quebec, if the government were spending $20,000 or $3,000 on a building at Grosse lie the work would not be overseen by this clerk of works? The department must put on a man who would be there every hour of every day, in the case of an important building like that. X want to find out what these men do.

They visit the building during the course of construction, oversee the work.
Mr. FOSTER, Then he looks after making repairs on all public buildings in course of construction occasionally, and reports with reference to them. To whom does he report ?

Directly to the chief arcli-tect of the department.
Mr. FOSTER, Is he kept pretty busy ?
They have got plenty to do on the kind of work the hon. gentleman has just mentioned, where they represent the department.
Now with reference to the plans of all these buildings, are they made in Ottawa ?
Yes. There are instances v, here the department employs outside architects to make the plans and supervise. In all these cases the architects themselves do the whole work.
Supposing you are building a $20,000 post office in Quebec ?

In that case it would be
done here.
The architects in the department here make the whole of the plans for that building ?
Almost invariably. But there are instances in which we employ an outside architect to make the plans, but that is not the rule. AVe keep our staff here for that purpose.
Now after you have prepared the plans and let the contract, do you employ a local architect for that building ?
Very often.
Do you also employ a man to oversee the work ?
Not where there is an architect.
When you employ an architect who does not oversee the work, how do you pay him ?
AVe pay him by commission, and from that commission he is supposed to employ a man on the work continually.

That is to say, in some cases. In the cases of all these buildings the plans of which are drawn here and where you do not employ an architect and a clerk of works, so to speak, locally, then, there is no other architect there but the government architect ; none that have anything to do with that building ?

No men who are paid by this vote.
Mr. FOST'E. I am speaking of men whom you employ to see that the architect's plans lire carried out in the construction of the building ; that is a clerk of works, so to speak, temporarily there while the building is being erected. In that case you do not employ an architect ?
No.
Then you appoint a man who is to see that the building is constructed according to the architect's plans. In that case you employ of course a mechanic ?
We always do, a man, for instance, understanding masonry or carpentering.

Where extensive repairs are undertaken in the public buildings of a province such as we have been voting many thousands of dollars for, or where a public building is to be modified or improved, are the plans made beforehand in the department here ?
All made in the department here.

Who reports as to the necessity and approximate cost of those repairs ? This year we have voted about $200,000 for repairs and improvements on public buildings in the province of Quebec. These must have been preceded by a report to the minister showing a necessity for these repairs and an estimate of the cost. Who is that done by ?

That comes from the department who are using the building. For instance, in post office improvements the reauest would come from the Post Office Department asking for certain repairs or additions to be made. Then tiie Public Works Department have a staff here who prepare the plans for those works, repairs or additions.

I understand the call for repairs or improvements comes from the department interested. But before the estimate is placed before us, who gives to the government a report of the probable cost, and the necessity and extent of those repairs ?
The chief architect of the department.
Then he visits these places in order to prepare the estimate ?
He cannot personally visit all the places, but some members of the staff are sent to each of these places.

Then when the repairs are finally decided upon, who superintends the work of carrying them out ? For instance, we have voted $25,000 to make some changes in the front part of the post office in Montreal ?

That would be overlooked by the agents of the department in the different cities. In the city of Montreal we have a local man who is paid out of this vote we are discussing; in that case he would overlook the repairs.
I heard the name of Mr. B61and mentioned for Quebec ; who is the man in Montreal 1
Mr. C. Desjardins is in charge in Montreal.
Who is the man who performs the same duty in Toronto ?

Mr. Hamilton is in charge of all the buildings there, in so far as the employees are concerned. We generally employ Mr. -Currie, the architect there, to make the plans, or to consult with in case of any renewals or repairs.
I am speaking more especially of repairs.
Mr. Currie generally overlooks the repairs of the department there.
A lot of repairs took place last year in the Toronto post office, who was the person ?
Mr. Currie, the architect.

In the case my hon. friend brought to the attention of the minister a few moments ago, the Macleod post oflice, Northwest Territories, I see the contract price is $13,973, and the clerk of works got $1,464 ; making for the architect and clerk of works $2,879. Is not that rather a high commission ? I want to ask the hon. minister this question : Has he not in his department officers who can prepare these plans without engaging an outside architect ? These are buildings that are being erected every day almost. New towns are springing up, appropriations are made and a_ court house that is suitable in one town is suitable in another town with very little alteration. Surely, when this Fort Macleod building was put up, the hon. gentleman had in his department plans and specifications suitable for that building without employing an outside architect at a cost of $1,415.
There is no architect.
Yes, Martel & Dangelier, $1,415.
Those are the heating contractors.

Those were heating contractors ? On this point I would like an answer from the hon. minister as to what the policy of the government is. Are we to understand that when a building is to be constructed in Macleod, for example, the department have plans and specifications that would be suitable for a town of that size, or are we to understand that special plans are made for each town ?

The hon. gentleman will know that it depends altogether on the question of the site. It is almost impossible to have a plan that is equally suitable for two sites. Very little alteration makes it necessary practically to make a new plan. The policy of the department has been to do all that work in the department. But we cannot follow that policy at all times. There are occasions when we employ an outside architect, in which case he has the supervision of the building, and is paid a percentage for his work ; yet, in all those cases in which an outside architect is employed, his plans are sent to the department and examined by the chief engineer before anything is done.
Who is Camille Desjardins, who does the work mentioned by my hon. friend a moment ago in the city of Montreal, and how long has he acted in that capacity ?

About fifteen years. He is a brother-in-law of Mr. Justice Ouimet, and was appointed by him.

'Mr. MONK. What is his remuneration ?
Construction of armouries, $50,000.
Is that the first construction ?
This is a vote that has been in the estimates for some years. It Is asked for by the Militia Department for the purpose of constructing small armouries in different places.
What armouries are proposed to be constructed ?
I have no demand from the department as yet for these armouries to be constructed out of this particular vote.

Does the hon. minister think it is quite proper to come down here and ask for a lump sum of $50,000 or $100,000 when he has not even decided that the armouries are required ? That is no proper voting of money. You should not ask for a vote unless you have outlined what uses you propose putting it to, and are able to give details to a certain extent. This bulk sum voting of $50,000 or $100,000 and placing it in a minister's hands, especially those of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden), would never do at all.
The hon. gentleman will understand that contracts have been made, for which a certain amount of this vote will have to be used.
Give an explanation of that.
I am speaking of the new ones. That does not take up the whole vote.
What are those contracts, and what do they amount to ?
They are for armouries at Kaslo, Fredericton and Broekville.
What is proposed to be done at Kaslo ?
I see that Kaslo was completed out of this year's expenditure.
Well, drop that out.
The places at which these armouries are to be erected are Burford and Fredericton, and there is some expenditure at Broekville.
What is the expenditure for these three ?
What is going on at Bur-ford ?
An armoury is being erected.

Why is not the construction of an armoury at Burford, where you
are spending $30,000, detailed here just the same as in those other cases in which you are making expenditures of from $10,000 to $30,000 ?
Mr., HYMAN. This is just a small expenditure.
No ; the expenditure is not $30,000. That is the expenditure for Burford and Fredericton together.
What is the expenditure at Burford ?
And at Fredericton ?
$12,000. And then there will be heating, electrical wiring and contingencies. The cost of the two buildings will be in the neighbourhood of $30,000.

That is what I understand. The hon. minister wants a vote for the construction of armouries of $50,000. A question brings out the fact that you are spending $9,900 on an armoury at Burford and $12,000 on an armoury at Fredericton. These expenditures may be all right, but what answer is there to the question : Why, instead of having it blindly for the construction of armouries, the minister should not have a vote for each, and should not put down ' armoury at Burford, $9,900 ' and ' armoury at Fredericton, $12,000 ' ? That is the way, I think, my hon. friend will admit it ought to be put in, and I would move that it be amended in that direction. Let us have it by all means in the vote, because you might as well just simply say : Here is $500,000 for the construction of armouries ; but that is not the way that votes ought to go through the House of Commons. There ought to be a definite building for which each vote is taken. In the way of repairs it is difficult to do that, because there are small repairs running from $10 to $300 or $400, but this is for the construction of a building.
The policy of voting a lump sum for the purpose of constructing small armouries was adopted some years ago. I do not know whether it was adopted during the time of my hon. friend
I do not think so.

Well, three or four years at any rate and for this reason : Often times it is necessary to have accommodation which is not foreseen and cannot be foreseen perhaps, and it was thought desirable to vote a sum-I think we began with $35,000 or $40,000-to build armouries which would cost anywhere from $2,500 up to $10,000 each. It was considered to be good policy, the matter was discussed here and the House agreed to it and that is the reason, if it be a reasi

on, why this vote has been placed in the estimates. I think it is a good reason. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) who I am sorry to observe just now seems to have some want of confidence in me- I thought he had the very greatest confidence in me-made some reference to the fact that I was not here last evening. I think the criticism he made was perfectly fair ; I think the minister interested in votes ought to be here, but it so happened that I was not able to be here last night. My bon! friend (Mr. Foster) would have had an opportunity, had he been here during the last four or five years, of learning that a policy with reference to expenditures of this kind had been laid down. My hon. friend wanted to know what the policy of the department was. That was a perfectly proper question. If he had been here he would have known, because he would have heard it stated. Perhaps it would not be inopportune for me to read one or two statements which I made to the House some two or three years ago upon this very subject, and if the committee will bear with me for a moment I shall do so. In October 1903, my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blaln) asked a question and in answer to him I made this statement, which will be found at page 13084 in the last volume for that year. I then said :
My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) will understand that it is impossible to do this work all at once. It will involve between one and two million dollars, and perhaps more, to properly house the different militia corps throughout this country. We are going on as rapidly as possible throughout the country, and I assure my hon. friend that we are selecting the places in which these buildings are to be constructed on the advice of military men and from a non-partisan, a purely military point of view. With regard to the rural districts and the smaller towns, where there is only say, one unit, my idea is that we should construct a substantial building which can be headquarters, armoury and storehouse, and with a room sufficiently large for a lecture room, where the officers who take an interest in military matters can bring their men together in the evening, and, by means of blackboards and so on, illustrate military affairs and give necessary instruction. This is the idea I have, and that I hope to be able to hegin to carry out in the near future. My plan will include every village of any importance in the Dominion of Canada.
Later on I again discussed the matter and on the 8th day of October, I made this statement, which will be found at page 13403 of the same volume :
I have already referred to the importance of housing the militia. If we want to make the infantry force of this country what it ought to be, we must provide for every single unit, every company, sufficient accommodation for at least one hundred men where they may meet together and spend their evenings, using it as a sort of club room, and having blackboards and other means to educate themselves in the art of war. If you do that, you will excite renewed interest among the men, and you will Sir F. W. BORDEN.
get together and get the sympathy of the very best men in the community. You will not then have to worry over the question whether you are to pay them seventy-five cents or a dollar or fifty cents a day. It is not the money that brings that class of men out. It is the loyal spirit' in them and the desire to serve their country ; and all they will ask is the opportunity to acquire the necessary knowledge in order to do so.
I have read this simply to show that the matter lias been under consideration, and that the department has adopted a policy with reference to it. I may, however, say to the committee that I believe we should have at every company headquarters, the headquarters of every unit, as I have said before, a substantial building. I had hoped that such a building in the rural districts might be constructed for $2,500 for the smaller ones up to $5,000 or $6,000 or $7,000 and that for a total of between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 running over perhaps five, six or possibly ten years, which would not be felt very seriously in any one year, we might have the whole militia of the country on its present footing properly housed. I am bound to say-and the acting Minister of Public Works, I am sure, will not object to my saying so, that I have been disappointed in the cost of the buildings which have been constructed.
That is that they have cost more than you thought.
They have cost more than we thought they would, and more than I think they should have cost.
That is the trouble with public works; it always has been, it always has been.

I am glad to have the minister present. It is a great pity he was not present last night, but we will excuse his absence of last night because he has acknowledged handsomely that he should have been here. That is a business view which we will take. I am sorry, too, that I have to put him to the trouble of spending 15 minutes going over wliat he has gone over before. He has to do it because I was not in the House last parliament. It was not my fault that I was not in the House and if he has been caused any trouble let him fight it out with the Postmaster General, who is peacefully reposing just ahead of him, for I believe he is largely instrumental in having prevented my presence here. I believe it was mainly through the kindly offices of the Postmaster General that I was deprived of being here during the last three or four years, and that consequently I have been obliged to trouble the Minister of Militia for fifteen minutes repetition of what he stated a few months ago. It is just that kind of light, thrown upon the subject by the minister who has the initiation of the votes, that helps the committee to understand what these votes are for, I said there was chronic trouble in the Public Works Department. It was so in my time. There was a continuous struggle of this kind-and I dare say that those ministers who have large works to construct experience the same difficulty today-that whereas as a business man you want to put up for a corps of one hundred men a storehouse and shelter, which a business man would put up for $2,000 or $2,500, when you come to have it done by the Public Works Department it would run up to $6,000 or $8,000. That is true with reference to post offices and public buildings of every kind. As business men and citizens of a common country, which is growing rapidly and in which the expenditures are enlarging in different ways, we must come to the conclusion that we shall have pretty hard times ahead of us to meet all the services of the country if we do not bring these down to an economical basis. I have every sympathy with the idea of having the militia of this country well cared for and having every one of these units provided with a home of its own ; but if you are going to do that, you have to get rid mighty quickly of the idea of spending $50,000, $60,000. $70,000 or $80,000 on these places. You cannot furnish ail these units with proper accommodation under $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 if you go on in this way. That is what I meant last night when I asked where we would come out at if the minister proceeded on a fixed line of providing for all at that rate. We can give all these units decent housing if we make up our minds to put up businesslike buildings. I think that is an excellent idea of the Minister of Militia ; and if the Postmaster General and the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Public Works, with reference to their various constructions, were to have a sort of international conference at Ottawa in which they would get together with their officers and compare notes and bring matters down to a business level, they would economize more than they are doing now and would serve the country very much better. Mind you, I am not criticising in any carping spirit any expenditure for the necessary services of the country. We have to have them and more of them. But I remind the committee that we are at this moment setting up sister provinces and furnishing them, that this is going to cost this country a large amount of money, that our services are reaching out to distant places, and that these are becoming more costly. Therefore, we ought to set our houses in some sort of economical, businesslike order, and have the expenditures carried out in such a careful and reasonable way that the general distribution in the end shall not overburden the country to such an extent that we shall at some time get Heightened at it or find it impossible and have to stop the very thing that we might have carried on if we had carried it on in a reasonable and economical way. Probably all ministers and governments make mistakes in that way. but every year makes it a more vital question with us in our growing country, and I am glad to hear the minister say he is proposing something of the kind. I do not forget that the Minister of Militia is on pledge that in the selection of sites for militia purposes he will act on the principle, not that Thomas or John or somebody else who has given good service to the party asks for something, but because it is necessary for the service. If I have caused the Minister of Militia and Defence trouble in asking for an explanation, the onus rests upon the interesting gentleman who sits beside him, the hon. Postmaster General.

I am very glad that my hon. friend gave me the opportunity to make the statement which I have made, and I assure him that it was no trouble, particularly, as I have found that the seed I have disseminated has fallen on such good ground. I am glad to find that, after all, my hon. friend has not such a want of confidence in me as I might have been led a few moments ago to suppose he had. With regard to the large expenditure in the great centres, there are in the city of Toronto, for instance, probably forty units.
I am not quaiTelling with a large expenditure in large centres.

The large expenditure there is perfectly justifiable. The same is true of Montreal, Hamilton and other large centres. I do not think any one will complain of that. But we have to construct in the country districts in order to house the militia properly six or seven hundred buildings, because we have at least one thousand units. I think it is quite as important, perhaps more important, that we should provide places where these units can meet and spend their evenings profitably, than it is even in the cities. As I pointed out in my remarks of two years ago, I think it is of the utmost importance to the welfare of the rural militia that this should be done as soon a possible, and, as my hon. friend has pointed out, it cannot and will not be done unless we are able to do it at a much lower rate of expenditure than we have been involving the country in up to the present time. I think that with from $2,500 to $7,500, possibly $10,000, we ought to be able to get all the accommodation required for one, two, and in some cases three, companies in a country district.

I would draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact that in the village of Colborne complaint is made that the cavalry corps there, has no place in which to store its guns and other equipments, Although the town is not a large one, this corps should be furnished with some place in which to store its equipment.
T think at present it has to store them in Coburg. I heard one of the officers say last summer that they had not a cartridge in their possession. I thought it rather strange that we should have a cavalry corps there and yet not have a cartridge among them. That would be rather awkward if any trouble should arise. I would also draw attention to the fact that there is a militia corps in Brighton, and that in Brighton there is no place in which that corps can store its equipment. I have never had any ambition in the soldiering line, but as the representative of the people I am prepared to vote for any reasonable expenditure to house and equip these men properly and also to pay them for their services. I think they have been underpaid. and if they get enough now I am very glad of it. So long as economy and business like methods are practised, I think that our militia should be furnished with these things and above all with ammunition to use if necessary.

The place to which my hon. friend refers is exactly one of these where a building of the kind I have described should be and will be constructed. With regard to the ammunition,
I have no doubt that there is ammunition not very far away from the headquarters.

As a representative of a rural constituency, I was much pleased to hear the remarks of the hon. Minister of Militia, I am glad to hear that he has outlined a policy by which he proposes to take care of the rural battalions. In the votes we have been giving to the militia for the building of armouries, it did strike me that all the money was going to the large towns and cities and that the rural battalions were being completely neglected. The county of Haldimand has one of the best battalions in the province. 1 am told that the 37tli battalion is probably the best of those that go to the Niagara camp. Yet, in the whole county there is not one drill shed for that battalion. I hope that the hon. minister will see his way clear to furnish us with some drill halls in that county. The town of Dunnville, where I reside, is a large, prosperous and growing town, and it has a splendid volunteer corps. I have received a number of letters already, since I have been in the House, from Dunnville, asking me to bring this matter before the House so that the hon. minister might know that the company in Dunnville have no place in which to drill or store their arms, but have to rent a place and pay for it out of their own pockets. The officers are very anxious that a drill hall should be built there. I can not refrain from complimenting the hon. minister on the policy he has outlined, and I hope he will not forget that good old county of Haldimand when he is distributing armouries and drill sheds.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I intended last evening, when the militia votes were being put through, to say a few words, but refrained from doing so as the hon. minster was absent. However, now that he is here I wish to draw his attention to some facts. I share in the pleasure of my hon. friend from Haldimand at the announcement of the minister that he intends to house all the militia in the rural districts, villages and towns. Gananoque is an important town. We have there a field battery, one of the oldest and best in the Dominion. We have also a rifle corps. A few years ago they had comfortable quarters containing a drill shed and an armoury, but my hon. friend tore that down and purchased another site. It was the intention of the government to provide housing for that corps but for some reason or other nothing was done, although ten years have elapsed.
Sir FREDERICK BORbEN. Not so long as that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
It was in 1896-nine years anyway. I have asked repeatedly to have our boys housed again. They have had to rent an old warehouse in the centre of a lumber yard where the guns are stored as well as the harness and other accoutrements, but they have only room to run the guns in and no place suitable for the men

at all. I beg to draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact, and would urge on him the necessity of providing without delay an armoury in the town of Gananoque. I am sure my hon. friend has waited long enough now, and I hope that he will see that a sum is put in the supplementaries to provide for sUch a building. The site was purchased and paid for some eight or ten years ago, and nothing done yet. I referred to another matter last night when the hon. minister was not present nor was the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty). But I had a conversation with that hon. gentleman afterwards, and he said he would remind the. minister of the necessity of having the Martello towers at Kingston, which were injured a few winters ago by the wind storms, put in respectable repair. We have Americans coming to Kingston by the thousands every year, and it is certainly no credit to us that these towers should remain there with their tops blown off and in a dilapidated condition. I hope that the hon. minister will, the first thing this spring have these Martello towers repaired, otherwise they may tumble down altogether.

Is a part of this vote to be expended for the purpose of erecting an armoury in Burford village ? Burford is a flourishing village which has a very good company of dragoons. This company has no armoury or drill hall, but there is a building in course of erection. Might I ask the hon. minister what has been expended and what further will be expended on the armoury at Burford ?
The contract for the Burford armoury it $9,900. That will complete the building.

I would like to take advantage of the presence of the Minister of Militia to draw his attention to the Toronto drill shed. This $40,000 for the extension of a drill hall is a revote. I asked the question when this contract would be commenced, also the nature of the work and in what direction the extension of the drill hall would be made. It was pointed out, that, a year ago when this appropriation was put in the estimates, the then minister of Public Works stated that the work would be proceeded with at once, in fact he said, the plans would be perfected in a few days from that date-March 2, 1904- and immediately the plans were completed and the frost sufficiently out of the ground the work would proceed. I think the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) knows better than any man in this country the immediate necessity for better drill hall accommodation in Toronto and the unpleasantness and difficulty among the regiments that has arisen because of the inadequacy of the present hall for all the troops there. The question is one of immediate importance to the militia men of Toronto.
They have waited long for this extension, and they are anxious to know when it will commence, what direction it will take, and generally what it will be.

I am not able to answer all my hon. friend's questions, but I think my colleague the Minister of Public Works will be able to give any information I cannot give. I wish to say, in a general way, that I consider the giving of additional accommodation to the militia force of Toronto a matter of the most urgent necessity. And, so far as I am concerned, I will continue to impress upon the Public Works Department the importance of giving that accommodation at the earliest possible moment. While I am not charged with the preparation of the plans and have not really examined them. I am told that an agreement or understanding has been reached, between the gentleman at the head of the engineering branch of my department and the chief architect of the Public Works Department, on a plan which will give ail the accommodation that is required for the Toronto garrison. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will be able to tell the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) when the work will be commenced.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What about Gananoque ?

I had intended to reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) when somebody intervened. I can only repeat the assurance I gave the committee a little while ago, that we will proceed with the construction of public buildings for the accommodation of the militia in accordance with the most urgent requirements of the service in different localities as decided upon by the officers of the Militia Council. With regard to Kingston, I am glad attention has been called to that matter. That pertains to my own department exclusively. We have a vote out of which can be taken the sum necessary to make these repairs, and I will see that it is done.

I wish to say a few words concerning the condition in this regard of the county' I have the honour to represent, the county of Bruce. We have what our people consider a very good regiment in that county, without any accommodation whatever except small rooms, provided at low rentals, at the company centres. The policy of the Minister of Militia, as lie has enunciated it to-night, has been laid before our people, and they very much approve of it. They are looking to the department now for more suitable accommodation for the regiment there, and I hope that when the minister is preparing his estimates he will not forget the great county of Bruce and will not give all the money to the cities and the portions of the country farther east. We in the west, look on ourselves as belonging to the fighting

races,-and we want consideration for our militia in that western part of Ontario.

We in this House must know that we owe a very great debt to the county of Bruce for sending such a very able representive as it has to this House. I am glad to hear from him that the policy which was first outlined two or three years ago is approved by that county. I can only say what I have said before, that we will take this matter up and we will see to it that Bruce is not neglected-of course, in the order of merit.

I join with the others in expressing my pleasure at the presence of the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) to-night. Last night, while the items for armouries throughout the province of Ontario were under consideration I brought up the subject of the armoury for the town of Cornwall. I pointed out to the Minister of Public Works the great importance of the eastern district, and the splendid battalion in the counties of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry, and the fact that that regiment was without a building even to store their arms. I stated that we in that section were very moderate. We quite agree with the proposition laid down by the Minister of Militia. We do not wish to see any such extravagant expenditure as that made in the town of Brockville, and then have the battalion disband and have a monument there to the Militia Department or the Public Works Department in the form of a building which cost, I think, in the neighbourhood of eighty or a hundred thousand dollars and is used only for social entertainments. and bazaars. We have in Cornwall a live battalion, one that is a credit to the province of Ontario. The officers of that department have waited on the Minister of Militia from time to time. They have not received from him any definite promise that I know of. They waited on the ex-Minister of Public Works, and that gentleman gave them a positive assurance that that armoury would be erected. Not only that, but he visited the town of Cornwall and went over the sites pointed out to him by the gentlemen who were extending to him the courtesies of the town. He approved of one site. The citizens naturally expected that the contract would be let immediately afterwards and that by this time they would have had a building ample for the purpose. Yet nothing has been done. The battalion feel very much aggrieved that they have been neglected. As I pointed out last night, the officer who is in charge of the battalion is a most active supporter of this government. My opponent in the last election is also an officer of that battalion and as I understand, a very capable officer indeed. He also. I believe, feels disappointed that nothing has been done. We had from the Minister of Public Works last night an assurance that Mr. p. h. mckenzie.
it would come. If he had said not only that it would come, but that it would come within a certain period, I would have been satisfied with that and would not have had anything to say to-night.
Now that the Minister of Militia is here-[DOT] he knows that the case is urgent. He knows that the officers and prominent citizens of the town have waited upon him several times urging that this building should be constructed. Perhaps he would be able to supplement the assurance I have received from tlie Minister of Public Works, and state definitely whether some .portion of this $100,000 that we are now discussing is to be expended in Cornwall to erect a suitable building. As I have said, we are very modest. An expenditure of $8,000 or $10,000, I think, would be ample to provide accommodation for the 59tli Battalion. I hope the Minister of Militia will give me definite assurance to-night that the building will be put under way this year.

My hon. friend (Mr. Pringle) is perhaps not aware- I do not know that he is a military man- that the regiment to which he refers is a rural battalion and not a city battalion. It is a battalion composed of eight companies, two of them and not more than two, have their headquarters in the town of Cornwall ; the remaining companies or units have their headquarters in probably six different places in that county, and perhaps the adjoining county. A few years ago it was recommended to the department that there should be a central armoury for country battalions, and that there should be one armoury alone for eight companies. That was found not to work, and that policy has been changed ; in fact we have reverted to the old system of keeping arms at company headquarters. I may say to my hon. friend that I agree with him absolutely that there should be a building procured or constructed in the town of Cornwall, but it will be of the kind that I have described, and which I am glad to observe he is reasonable enough to be satisfied with, a moderate building which would also give accommodation for regimental headquarters. I would suggest that Cornwall being a growing town, probably we might provide for two companies additional, having in view the future. Subject to what I said a moment ago, that these matters must all be decided by the Militia Council, by the expert advisers of the militia and of the government, I think I can give the assurance that it will not be very long at any rate before provision is made for the regiment to which my hon. friend refers.
Mr. LALOR, I notice that some hon. gentlemen who have spoken asking for drill halls for their counties have received assurances from the Minister of Militia that drill halls will be built for them. I have not been fortunate enough to draw that promise from the Minister of Militia as to

whether he will remember Haldimand county. I have already complimented him on the policy he has outlined, it is a wise policy and in the interests of the rural militia. I think the great difficulty with rural battalions in the past has been that they have not received the attention they deserved. In fact my predecessor in this House not long ago alluded to the rural battalions as being the shadow of a shadow of a skeleton.
