That was not very complimentary to the rural battalions, especially as coming from a military gentleman himself. Now I hope the Minister of Militia will improve that state of affairs, and rejoice the hearts of the battalion of Haldimand county that I have the honour to represent, by promising that he will build a drill hall in the town of Dunnville.

The appeal of my hon. friend is quite irresistible. If T did not refer especially to the county of Haldimand, it was not out of discourtesy, but because some one intervened before I had had an opportunity of speaking. I will only repeat what I have said, that I believe the county of Haldimand is one that is especially deserving as the regiment of that county is especially deserving. 1 have had the pleasure of seeing that regiment on many occasions, and it will give me a great deal of pleasure if the Militia Council should recommend my hon. friend's town as one of the early towns to receive a building of this kind.
Am I going to be left out ?
Would the minister tell us what he is going to do with the Toronto work ?

I explained last night that there are two works to be done in Toronto. Orie is the enlargement of the armoury, putting another story on the armoury to be used for storing the arms. The plans and specifications are now in the hands of the printers, and as soon as they are received tenders will be advertised for. As regards the other and larger work, the plans I understand are to be sent over to the Militia Department, whence they will be forwarded to Toronto to the officers there to pass upon ; then they will come back to the Department of Public Works. All that of course will take some time. As the building will be a large one costing some $250 000, it will tak<>
some time to prepare the plans and specifications.
Is it the intention of the department to proceed with this work ? Last year we were told the same thing, we were told the plans would be finished in two days.

I think the hon. gentleman must have been mistaken, and that the minister had reference to plans for an addition, that is, putting on an extra story where the
arms are to be stored. I cannot conceive that he referred to the larger work.
I understand it is the intention of the government to proceed with this building in due course ?
Without question.
What Is being done in Fredericton V $12,000 of that vote I think is devoted to the armoury in Fredericton.
That is for restoring the building that was burnt.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Militia to the condition of the drill hall at Summerside. I have had several conversations with the hon. gentleman last year on this subject, and I had his assurance that the matter would be looked into and possibly something would be done. Up to the present there has been no move made. If it is the desire of the minister to have the efficiency of the different companies up to standard, and to keep up the interest of the rural and small town companies, he will have to provide better accommodation than we have in the town of Summerside. As I pointed out last night, we have an old building forty or fifty years old on our public square, with no floor and absolutely no accommodation.
' Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. It is true that my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) called my attention to the matter last year, and I had one of my officers visit the place and make a report upon the building. The question is now before the department for action. I hope that in the near future some action will be taken. I would like to add in this connection that it is impossible that all these buildings should be erected at once. I may be permitted to remark that in my own county we have a regiment of infantry of eight companies and two squadrons of cavalry, yet we have only an old wooden drill hall in the town of Kentville, which was built many years ago. There has not been a thousand dollars expended on buildings to house the militia in my county during the nine years I have been a minister. I teil my people that they must be patient. The time will come, I hope, when they will all be housed and I will ask some of my hon. friends to emulate my example and be patient.
We would almost prefer in my town to wait a year or two, if we had the assurance that a suitable building would he put up, and one which would at the same time be an ornament to the town.

Before we proceed further, there was one item left over in the Ontario list, on the understanding that the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence would make a statement in regard to it. I refer to the Woodstock armoury. I suppose there is no objection to passing that item ?

All right.
Ottawa public buildings, including repairs, ventilation and lighting, furniture, &c., $140,000.
What is this ? There was a vote last night for this same thing.

Oh, no ; but there was really a discussion upon this vote last night. This is the usual vote for the care of the buildings.
Rents-Dominion public buildings, $64,000.
Are these all in Ottawa ?
No ; the Ottawa rents amount to $4,7,111. These are the rents which the department pays for rented buildings throughout Canada.

I suppose these rents have to be paid as the leases are made ? I know the hon. gentleman had personally nothing to do with the renting of these buildings, but I hope he will be able to give us some assurance that he will stop this system. I think that probably, individually, we would all concede that the present system is a mistake. The government have rented buildings all over the city ; they have rented some good buildings and some poor buildings, and the rents are all high. Rumour says on the street that some of the rents are very high even for individuals to pay, but taking into consideration the rate of interest that the government have to pay for money, all of these rentals are high. I think that individually the hon. minister and all other members of the House will probably agree that if the government need all this accommodation they ought to provide it in some other way. They should erect a building. There is plenty of land in Ottawa, and the government could erect a fine building at no greater annual charge for interest than the rental which they are now paying. They are paying interest on about $2,000,000 in rentals for these buildings that they are now occupying, whereas they could buy land below the Supreme Court and erect a building there. I hope the minister will give us some assurance that he will not follow the system pursued by his predecessor in this regard.

I promised the committee at a previous sitting to make a statement in regard to this question. I quite agree that the time has come when the government should have a definite policy in regard to making provision for the different departments of government. It requires a considerable amount of material to be got together, details of space and everything of that kind. The architect of the department is at present engaged upon the matter, and I hope before the session is over to lay before the House some plan so that we may get rid of the large payments of rent, and Mr. HYMAN.
house each department in a building belonging to the government.
Is it the intention of the hon. jninister to try and arrange so that he will not have to lease any more buildings in Ottawa ?

I cannot say that, because, in the meantime, if there are applications made by any department for more room, and it is found by the Department of Public Works that they must have room, of necessity we must rent a building. But I promise that there will be no long leases, and that there will be no leases that cannot be got rid of when we are ready to go into a new building.

It is not only the question of money, but the question of extreme inconvenience that is experienced by the public when a department is divided up between two or three different buildings. The minister at the head of the department perhaps knows where the various branches are, but it is pretty hard for any other person to find the branch which he wants.
How much is being paid for rent for the building occupied by the Railway Commission ?

The whole of that makes up $64,000 ?
No ; that is just for buildings in Ottawa, making a total of $47,111.
Reverting to the preceding item, there is an increase of $15,000. The hon. minister has not explained the cause of that.
That is on account of the larger number of buildings. The care of the buildings we rent as well as of the buildings we own is included in that vote, and there are more buildings now to take care of.

The hon. gentleman stated that the policy would be to make short leases in future until the question of the erection of a larger building is settled. May I ask the hon. minister if any of the leases he has read over are long leases ?
The Woods building is the only one that can be called a long lease ; that has some seven years to run.
In the new short leases has the department done anything towards repairs or fixing up ?
That will come out of the vote previous to this ; this vote is simply for the rent.

Quite a large sum was spent by the government on the building at the corner of Metcalfe and Slater streets to put it in shape for the census department to use. In addition to that there is a large payment for rent. What I want to get at is whether the same policy has been carried out in this long list.

The only newly arranged building in which a large amount has been spent is the Corry building. In that there is no expenditure that we could not remove. All the other buildings are outside of the city of Ottawa.
Do the owners of buildings in Ottawa leased by the government have to pay any taxation to the city of Ottawa ?
In the only lease I have made I have insisted on having in the lease a clause to the effect that the taxes must be paid. That policy will be followed while I am in the department.
The taxes must be paid to the city of Ottawa by the owner of the building.
Yes.

In view of the fact that no taxes are paid to the city did the owner of the Census building make any substantial reduction in the rent to the government ? Did the government insist on such a low rate to which they were surely entitled ?

The proposition the hon. gentleman makes is a perfect business one, and I presume that was taken into consideration. I did not personally conduct the negotiations for these leases. They were discussed very fully.

I am glad to hear what the minister says about the payment of taxes and 1 hope he will make a change in regard to the renting of buildings. There is no doubt that some of these leases have been made at altogether too high a price and that the government is paying more than a private individual would pay in Ottawa for the same building. I do not know who is to blame for it, in the past, but I think the hon. gentleman is right in seeing that the city of Ottawa gets the taxes from any buildings which he rents in the future. I only hope that he will see that the government does not in the future pay exorbitant rentals such as have been paid for some of these buildings in the past.

Some new legislation was passed by the Ontario legislature last session to the effect that all public buildings in future shall be assessed and liable to taxation. I am not quite sure of the details of the Bill but it might be worth while to look it up.
Yukon public building, $105,000.
That is a large sum.

I have all the details of the expenditure here. I shall refer to one item so that the committee will understand the reason of the large expenditure. It is on account of the salaries being very large. For instance the post office. We are obliged to pay the caretaker $160 a month, practically three times the amount we would pay here. A charwoman there gets $150 a month.
And a living allowance ?

No. Then there is lighting $1,500, fuel which is very high $2,500, and repairs and maintenance, another large item. The Public Works Department have taken over all of this work. Heretofore a part of this vote was voted by the House to the Interior Department, but now the j Public Works Department have taken the I whole vote and are endeavouring to exercise

What is the cost of the electric light to the government?
About $17,000. For the first three thousand lights we pay $2.25 per light per annum, and tor all over three thousand, $2 per light, each lamp being of 16-candle power.

How did you come at that flat rate? You must have done it on some plan other than the rule of thumb. You must have ascertained pretty nearly the cost of generation, and fixed the rate accordingly, allowing the company its reasonable profit.
The power of the lamps was tested.

The department knows or ought to know what it costs to make each of these lights. Then, the question would come up, is it cheaper to buy the light or to generate it ? Having ascertained the cost of generation, how much profit do we pay over and above that?

I have not got the figures.
Mr. FOSTER, Will the minister look into that?
I will. I think it is a very proper question.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You supply all the wiring and all the breakages and give $2 a light for the power?
Yes.

During a certain number of months the lights are not used, a large number are very little used and many, 1
venture to say, are never used. Is the government paying $2 per light for those which are not used at all ?
Mi-. HYMAN. There is no doubt about
that, just as in your own house you would pay so much a light whether you used it or not
There is a vast difference between the two.
Would it not be possible to measure all the light used, and pay for it according to the amount consumed ?
Undoubtedly it would.

This city used to have a flat rate system, and those who had lights burnt them all night without paying any extra cost, but the companies do not permit that kind of thing to be done now. They have adopted the meter system. I suppose that is more profitable to the companies.

It may be, but the business system, both for the company and the consumer, is that the consumer should pay for what he actually uses. A flat rate saves a lot of trouble and may be better for the consumer in some cases, but the honest way is to measure everything and pay for just what you use, especially in an immense establishment like this, where you have so many lights that are not used all the time and so many used a very little part of the year. You are paying a flat rate, and may, on the whole, not be paying over much, but what I want to get at is the actual amount used, if it can be ascertained, and so come down to the basis of cost and profit.
I shall be very glad to have the matter looked into.
Is the contract let yearly?
It is a 10-year contract. It is some seven years ago the contract was made.

Does the bon. minister get sixteen candle power ? I have a pretty strong suspicion that the lights are not up to that standard. I think the price Is not extravagant, having some little knowledge of the cost of electric lights, but I fear the lights are not up to the power claimed.

The arc lights are tested by the electricians of the department.
Ottawa public buildings-telephone service,
What number of telephones is used ?
Two hundred aud forty-eight.
What is the increase over last year ?
About ten or twelve.
Is there a -special rate charged ?
$35 per 'phone.
What is paid in the city ?
$45 for office telephones and $25 for house telephones.
Is not that excessive? In our little town we only pay the Bell Telephone Company $15 a year.

In the smaller towns telephone service is cheaper. Where you have connection with only 200 or 300 'phones, as in Petrolia, the cost is less than in a city, where you have connection with several thousands.
Has the hon. minister ever considered the possibility of having a system of departmental telephones on the automatic plan ?

I have given it casual consideration, but am asked by one of the de-
53J
partments to take the matter up, and will do so when I have the opportunity.

No doubt, if the hon. minister goes into it thoroughly, he will find the automatic system very much less expensive. I am not saying that because I have some connection with an automatic patent-I have not made anything out of it-but because I have had occasion to look into it, and believe it could be used to great advantage for the departmental service. You do not require anybody to look after the central office. It runs itself and is just as true, in fact truer, than the manual switch system, because that depends on human agencies. The other is a perfectly constructed machinery which will run any number of years, which is almost unwearable, and in which everything runs automatically. It has also this other great advantage, which will commend itself to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. He often wants to talk confidentially with one of his brother conspirators in some other department-the Postmaster General, for instance. He does not want any risk of being overheard. Well, the automatic system is absolutely secret. It is impossible for anybody to break in between the two who are talking. My hon. friend can see what great advantage that is.
I shall look into that matter.
That system was here a year or two ago in Ottawa.

There are half a dozen systems.

Is that for buildings all over the Dominion ?
Yes.

The Minister of Justice will move some Bills standing in his name, and then we shall go into supply. I understand the Minister of Inland Revenue will be prepared to proceed. If his estimates are completed, the Minister of Agriculture will take up some of his items, and, if these are finished, the Minister of Public Works will go on.
